sections.title: Human language and computation
Speech movements in MRI

teaching.text: **Real-time MRI films the inside of the head while a person talks.** This makes the hidden movements of speech visible. The view is a side view cut down the middle of the head. The face points left, and the back of the neck is on the right. Air appears black in the image. Soft tissue such as the tongue, lips and throat walls appears gray and white.
children: The **lips** sit at the far left. They open, close, round and spread during speech.

The **tongue** is the large rounded mass that fills most of the mouth. It is the most active structure in speech. It bunches up toward the roof of the mouth, pulls back toward the throat, or lies low.

The roof of the mouth has two parts. The front part is bony and is called the **hard palate**. The back part is soft and movable and is called the **soft palate** or **velum**. The soft palate lifts to seal off the nose, or lowers to let air flow out through the nose.
Behind the tongue, a dark channel of air runs down the throat. This channel is the **pharynx**. Below it sits the **larynx**, which holds the **vocal folds**.

teaching.text: **During speech, all of these structures move at the same time and at high speed.** The jaw rises and falls. The lips open and close. The tongue reshapes itself many times per second. The soft palate lifts and lowers.
children: Each sound depends on a precise shape of the whole passage. The shapes flow smoothly into one another.
The two movies capture the same speaker's vocal tract in two different shapes. The difference comes almost entirely from where the tongue and lips are placed.

sections.title: Why speech is a remarkable learned skill

teaching.text: **We learn to move our speech organs in extremely complex ways with no instructions and almost no visual feedback.** Nobody tells a young child where to put the tongue tip for a sound. A child cannot see their own tongue, soft palate or vocal folds, because those organs are hidden inside the mouth and throat.
children: **By ages 2 to 4**, children speak with a wide vocabulary and near-adult language. This happens with hardly any explicit instruction. Children pick up thousands of words and the rules for combining them just from being around people who talk.

**Reading and writing** follow a different path. A child may memorize the shapes of the letters early. Reading and writing whole words usually comes at **ages 6 to 7**, and it requires a great deal of instruction.

The contrast between the two is the point. Speech uses hidden organs that the learner cannot see, yet it develops almost on its own. Reading and writing use the eyes and hands, which are fully visible, yet they need years of teaching. So speech is a deep human cognitive skill that the brain is prepared to acquire.

teaching.text: **Articulatory phonetics is the field that studies the movements of the structures of the vocal tract.** The **vocal tract** is the full air passage used in speech. It runs from the larynx up through the throat and mouth to the lips, with a side branch into the nose.
children: Articulatory phonetics asks which structures move, where they move to, and how those movements create the different sounds of a language. Real-time MRI is one of its main tools.

teaching.text: **In the last two years, voice assistants and other speech technology have come to emulate human speech ability.** To **emulate** an ability means to reproduce its behavior. These systems now produce natural-sounding speech, and they recognize spoken language with high accuracy.
children: **LING 285 is about both human speech and AI speech.** One side studies how people produce and perceive speech. The other side studies how modern AI systems model that same ability. The two can then be compared directly.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics

teaching.text: **The next step is to focus on the air between the tongue and the rest of the vocal tract.** In the real vocal tract, that air space bends. It runs down the throat and then forward through the mouth. Ignoring the curve and straightening the passage turns the vocal tract into a simple **tube of air**.
children: One end of the tube is the **lips**. There the passage is open to the outside air. The other end is the **larynx** deep in the throat. There the tube is treated as closed. The walls of the tube stand for the tongue and the other surfaces around the air space.

The tube is labeled **schwa**. Schwa is the neutral relaxed vowel, the "uh" sound at the start of "about." For schwa, the tongue sits in a central resting position and does not narrow the passage much anywhere. So the air space is about the same width from end to end, and the straight even tube fits schwa best.

teaching.text: **The air inside the tube vibrates by shifting back and forth. It does not flow out the end.** Each small bit of air is drawn as a blue circle. Each column of circles shifts back and forth around its own resting position.
children: Where neighboring columns move toward each other, the air is squeezed together. This region is a **compression**, where the air is packed more tightly.
Where neighboring columns move apart, the air spreads out. This region is a **rarefaction**, where the air is packed more loosely.
These regions of packing and spreading travel along the tube and reflect back from its ends. This repeating pattern is the **vibration of air**. It makes up the sound of the vowel.

teaching.text: **Acoustic phonetics is the field that studies how air vibrates in the vocal tract and what sound results.** Articulatory phonetics describes the shape of the tube. Acoustic phonetics describes the physics of the air inside it. The two fields connect directly to each other. Moving the tongue and lips changes the shape of the tube, and changing the shape of the tube changes how the air inside it vibrates.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters

teaching.text: **AI brings real harms, and pretending it does not exist is not a workable option.** The harms are psychological, economic, social and environmental. Many scientists also warn about **existential harm**, meaning the possibility that advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival or basic way of life.
children: AI exists, with many harms and some benefits. One benefit is **immunotherapy**, which uses the body's own immune system to fight diseases such as cancer. Another is **environmental engineering**, the design of solutions to environmental problems.
The environmental case cuts both ways. Running large AI systems uses enormous amounts of energy. At the same time, AI tools are being applied to engineering problems that could help the environment.

teaching.text: **One of the biggest dangers is that we have no idea how AI works.** The phrase for this is "we know everything, and understand nothing."
children: "We know everything" means every number and every calculation inside an AI system can be inspected. People built the system, so they can look at all of its parts.
"We understand nothing" means that no one can explain why the system produces the particular answers it does, even with all of those details in hand.
Very few people know how these systems operate. That is a danger in itself, because decisions about how AI is built and used end up in very few hands.

teaching.text: **AI literacy is necessary for many groups of people.** AI literacy means a working understanding of what AI systems are and how they behave.
children: Scientists who use AI need it to judge whether their results are trustworthy. Politicians who need to control AI need it to write sensible rules. Lawyers who litigate cases involving AI need it to argue about what a system did and why.
The course is built on one belief. A creative thinker in a class like this one can help us understand these systems well enough to benefit from them while avoiding their negative consequences.

sections.title: Course goals

teaching.text: **The course has four specific goals.**
children: First, to appreciate the human cognitive skill of **speech**, which people acquire with almost no instruction.
Second, to understand some basic principles of **physics** through speech, such as how air vibrates inside the tube of the vocal tract.
Third, to understand how modern **AI systems model human cognition**, meaning how machines reproduce abilities such as speaking and understanding language.
Fourth, to sharpen **methodical reasoning** through **elementary programming**. Writing a simple program forces each step of a problem to be stated clearly and in the correct order.

teaching.text: **The course also has three general goals.**
children: First, to think creatively in a rich **interdisciplinary** way. The material draws on physics, psychology, linguistics, biology, economics, computer science, philosophy, neuroscience and many other fields.
Second, to deepen our understanding of the world we live in today, where AI systems are becoming part of daily life.
Third, to sharpen our **skillful use of modern AI systems**, with a clear sense of what they can and cannot do.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning

teaching.text: **Diotima's ladder describes the climb from surface knowledge toward deep understanding.** Surface knowledge is knowledge of particular things. Deep understanding is understanding of the general ideas behind them. Diotima, dated here to around 440 BCE, taught **Socrates** about this ladder in Plato's Symposium. Socrates taught **Plato**, and Plato taught **Aristotle**.

**The bottom of the ladder holds knowledge that comes from routine and copying.** This includes **daily experience, habit and memorization**. It also includes **specialized skills, repetition and replication**, and learning from **textbooks**.
children: The rule at this level is that **similar is same, and slight difference is different**. Things that look alike are treated as identical. Things that look a little different are treated as unrelated.

teaching.text: **The top of the ladder holds creativity, insight, thought, focus, attention, imagination and vision.** It also holds **problem-posing, problem-solving, critical reading and creative writing**.
children: The rule at this level is reversed. **Different can be same, and similar can be different.** Things that look different can share the same deeper structure. Things that look alike can be fundamentally different.

Speech gives a direct example. The sounds f and v sound different, yet they are made in the same place in the mouth. The th in "thing" and the th in "that" are spelled the same, yet one uses vocal fold vibration and the other does not.
**Problem-posing** means asking good questions in the first place. **Problem-solving** means answering questions once they have been asked.

teaching.text: **A person climbs the ladder through repeated cycles of question and answer.** Each cycle lifts understanding one rung higher. The cycles repeat again and again from the bottom to the top. This is the method Socrates became famous for.

**For about 2500 years, people could fake it.** They could do well by memorizing, repeating and replicating, without climbing the ladder. In 2026 that is no longer true. Interviews for jobs and graduate school now look for the properties at the top of the ladder.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives

teaching.text: **The quickest way to understand speech sounds is to produce them and notice what the body does.** The exercise uses four pairs of sounds. Each pair is held as one long sound that switches partway through.
children: Hold the **f** in "fat," then switch to the **v** in "vat." Hold the **th** in "thing," then switch to the **th** in "that." Hold the **s** in "sing," then switch to the **z** in "zing." Hold the **sh** in "mesh," then switch to the buzzing sound in the middle of "beige," written **j** here. It is not the j in "jump."

teaching.text: **Within each pair, the difference is voice. Voice is whether the vocal folds vibrate.** Rest the fingers lightly on the front of the throat while switching.
children: During f, the first th, s and sh, the throat stays still. The sound is a pure hiss of air.
During v, the second th, z and the sound in "beige," a buzzing vibration appears in the throat. The sound gains a humming quality.

The **vocal folds** are two small folds of tissue inside the larynx. When they are held apart, air passes through silently, and the sound is **voiceless**. When they are brought close together, the airflow makes them vibrate rapidly, and the sound is **voiced**.
Within each pair, the tongue and lips stay in the same position. Only the vocal folds change. So voicing is controlled separately from the mouth.

teaching.text: **From one line to the next, the difference is place of articulation. Place of articulation is where the narrowing that makes the sound is formed.**
children: For f and v, the lower lip presses against the upper front teeth. For both th sounds, the tongue tip touches the upper front teeth. For s and z, the tongue tip comes close to the ridge just behind the upper front teeth. For sh and the sound in "beige," the tongue pulls a bit further back.
Each new line moves the narrowing further back in the mouth.

teaching.text: **Voice and place of articulation are two separate, independent properties of a speech sound.** Every sound in the exercise can be described by stating both. Changing one while keeping the other fixed produces a different sound.

sections.title: The fricative system

teaching.text: **All of these sounds are fricatives.** A fricative is made by bringing two parts of the vocal tract very close together without closing the passage. Air from the lungs is forced through the narrow gap. The small opening makes the airflow turbulent. The turbulent flow produces the hissing or buzzing noise. The sound can be held as long as there is breath.

**The fricative table has voice in the rows and place of articulation in the columns.** The places are **labial, dental, alveolar and postalveolar**. The voiceless row holds f, th, s and sh. The voiced row holds v, th, z and j.
children: **Labial** means made with the lips. For f and v, the lower lip rises to touch the upper front teeth. Air hisses through the gaps between them. In the MRI, the lower lip is tucked under the upper teeth, and the tongue lies low.
**Dental** means made at the teeth. For the two th sounds, the tip of the tongue touches the upper front teeth. In the MRI, the front of the tongue is pushed forward to the teeth.

**Alveolar** means made at the **alveolar ridge**. The alveolar ridge is the small bony ridge on the roof of the mouth just behind the upper front teeth. For s and z, the tongue tip rises to form a narrow groove close to that ridge.

**Postalveolar** means made just behind the alveolar ridge. For sh and the sound in "beige," a wider section of the front of the tongue rises a little further back than for s. The lips often push slightly forward.

teaching.text: **Two fricatives in the same column differ only in voicing. Two fricatives in the same row differ only in place.** The two th sounds make this clear. English spells them the same way, yet one is voiceless and the other is voiced.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality

teaching.text: **Stops are made by closing the passage completely for a brief moment.** During the closure, no air can escape through the mouth. A fricative leaves a narrow gap open, and a stop does not.
children: While the closure is held, air from the lungs keeps pushing into the mouth. Pressure builds up behind the closure. When the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out. That burst makes a stop sound short and sharp.
A stop cannot be held as a continuous sound. Its sound depends on the closing and the release.

teaching.text: **The English stops form a grid of three places of articulation and three types.** Each row keeps one place and changes the type. Each column keeps one type and changes the place.
children: The first row is **p, b and m**. All three close the **lips**. For p, the vocal folds stay still. For b, the vocal folds vibrate. For m, the vocal folds vibrate and the **soft palate lowers**, so air flows out through the nose while the lips are closed.

The second row is **t, d and n**. All three press the tongue tip against the **alveolar ridge**, the same place used for s and z. For t, the vocal folds stay still. For d, the vocal folds vibrate. For n, the vocal folds vibrate and the soft palate lowers.

The third row is **k, g and ng**. All three raise the **back of the tongue** against the **soft palate**. For k, the vocal folds stay still. For g, the vocal folds vibrate. For ng, the sound at the end of "sing," they vibrate and the passage to the nose opens.

teaching.text: **The columns follow the same logic as the fricative table.** The first column, **p, t and k**, holds the **voiceless** stops. The second column, **b, d and g**, holds the **voiced** stops. The third column, **m, n and ng**, holds the **nasal** stops. Nasal stops are voiced, and they send air through the nose.
children: A sound made with the soft palate lowered is called a **nasal**. The MRI of m shows the gap opened between the soft palate and the back of the throat.
Nine sounds come from three places of closure combined with three settings of the vocal folds and soft palate. A small number of independent movements builds a large set of speech sounds.

lecture02.title: 02 · Speech structure and learning in AI

sections.title: Human language and technology
Lecture agenda
Internal coordination during speech

teaching.text: **Real-time MRI films the inside of the head while a person is talking.** The images are **midsagittal**, a side-view slice taken straight down the middle of the head, from the nose to the back of the neck. The face points to the left. The lips are on the left edge, and the spinal column is the bright vertical band on the right. Each recording runs about half a minute and includes the speaker's sound, so every movement can be matched to the speech it produces.
children: **Air shows up black** because it gives off almost no signal. Soft tissue such as the tongue shows up gray or white. So the dark spaces are the open airways. These are the mouth cavity, the nasal passages above the roof of the mouth, and the **pharynx**, the air tube at the back of the throat behind the tongue.

The large rounded gray mass filling most of the mouth is the **tongue**. Above it is the **hard palate**, the bony roof of the mouth. Hanging from the back of the hard palate is the **velum**, or soft palate. The velum can be raised or lowered to close or open the path from the throat into the nose.

teaching.text: **When the recordings play, the tongue, lips, jaw and velum all move at once and very quickly.** Every consonant and vowel we hear is the result of the speaker shaping this tube of air in a particular way. **Phonetics** is the study of these speech sounds. The images give a direct way to see the shapes behind them.

sections.title: Fricative place and voicing

teaching.text: **A fricative is a consonant made by bringing two parts of the mouth very close together without closing them completely.** Air is pushed through the narrow gap. The squeezed air becomes turbulent. This produces the hissing or buzzing noise in sounds like f and s. A fricative can be held for as long as there is breath.

**English fricatives are organized along two dimensions, place of articulation and voicing.** Place of articulation is where in the mouth the narrow gap is formed. Voicing is whether the **vocal folds** in the larynx vibrate while the sound is made.
children: A **voiceless** sound is made with the vocal folds apart and still. The only noise is the hiss of air through the gap.
A **voiced** sound is made with the vocal folds vibrating. The hiss is combined with a buzz. A hand on the throat feels vibration during "zzzz" and no vibration during "ssss."

teaching.text: **The English fricatives fall into four places of articulation. Each place has a voiceless member and a voiced member.**
children: **Labial** fricatives are f (voiceless) and v (voiced). Labial refers to the lips. For f and v, the lower lip is raised against the upper front teeth.
**Dental** fricatives are both spelled th. The voiceless one starts "think." The voiced one starts "this." The tip of the tongue sits against or just between the upper teeth.
**Alveolar** fricatives are s (voiceless) and z (voiced). The **alveolar ridge** is the bony ridge just behind the upper front teeth. The tongue tip is raised close to it.

**Postalveolar** fricatives are sh (voiceless) and its voiced partner written j, the sound in the middle of "measure." The gap is formed just behind the alveolar ridge, a little farther back than for s and z.

teaching.text: **The four MRI images line up with the four places. The constriction moves backward from one place to the next.** In the labial image, the lower lip is pulled up toward the upper teeth. In the dental image, the front of the tongue is pushed forward toward the teeth. In the alveolar image, the tongue tip is raised toward the ridge behind the upper teeth. In the postalveolar image, the narrowing sits slightly farther back.
children: Each pair is made with the **same place and the same manner**. The pairs are f and v, the two th sounds, s and z, and sh and j. The only difference within a pair is whether the vocal folds vibrate.

sections.title: Oral and nasal stop comparisons

teaching.text: **A stop is a consonant made by closing the vocal tract completely at some point.** Air cannot get out through the mouth. Air pressure builds up behind the closure. When the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out. English has two kinds of stops, **oral stops** and **nasal stops**.
children: In an **oral stop**, also called a **plosive**, the velum is raised against the back wall of the throat. This seals off the nose. With both the mouth and the nose closed, pressure builds and is released as a small burst of air.

In a **nasal stop**, the mouth is closed in exactly the same way, but the velum is lowered. Air flows out through the nose the whole time. So there is no pressure build-up, and the sound has a humming quality.

teaching.text: **The stops fall into three places of articulation. Each place has a voiceless oral stop, a voiced oral stop and a nasal stop.**
children: At the **lips**, p is voiceless, b is voiced, and m is the nasal. The MRI images for p, b and m all show the two lips pressed together.
At the **alveolar ridge**, t is voiceless, d is voiced, and n is the nasal. The images for t, d and n show the tongue tip pressed against the ridge behind the upper teeth.

At the **velum**, k is voiceless, g is voiced, and ng is the nasal, the sound at the end of "sing." A sound made at the velum is called **velar**. The images for k, g and ng show the back of the tongue humped up against the soft palate.

teaching.text: **The nasal images differ from the oral images in the position of the velum.** In m, n and ng, the velum hangs down away from the back of the throat. This leaves an open passage into the nose. In p, t and k, the velum is raised to seal that passage. The short clips show each closure forming and releasing in real time. So a stop is an event in time. First the closure, then pressure or nasal airflow, then the release.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge

teaching.text: **The fricatives and stops fit into one table built on three properties, manner of articulation, place of articulation and voice.** Manner of articulation is how the air is shaped. It can be a narrow gap, as in a fricative. It can be a full closure with the nose sealed, as in an oral stop. It can be a full closure with the nose open, as in a nasal stop.
children: The places run from the front of the mouth to the back. They are **labial, dental, alveolar, postalveolar** and **velar**.

The fricatives fill the labial, dental, alveolar and postalveolar columns, each with a voiceless and a voiced member. The oral stops fill the labial, alveolar and velar columns, with voiceless p, t and k and voiced b, d and g. The nasal stops fill the same three columns, and all of them are voiced.

teaching.text: **Every one of these consonants is a combination of three values.** The sound t is a **voiceless alveolar oral stop**. The sound z is a **voiced alveolar fricative**. Changing just one value produces a different sound. Changing t from voiceless to voiced gives d. Changing d from an oral stop to a nasal stop gives n.

**The empty cells are also informative.** None of these English consonants is a dental or postalveolar stop. None is a velar fricative. So the sounds of English are not a random collection of noises. They are a **highly structured system** of shared properties.
children: Every English speaker already uses this system every time they talk, without ever having been taught the table. So a speaker's knowledge of English contains a great deal of hidden structure, organized along place, manner and voice.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities

teaching.text: **Artificial intelligence is a model of five psychological skills that animals have.** The five skills are **knowing, recognizing, attending, acting** and **learning**.
children: Knowing is having information stored in a usable form. Recognizing is identifying something from the input that arrives. Attending is selecting which parts of the input to focus on. Acting is producing a behavior or output. Learning is changing over time based on experience.

teaching.text: **The way AI models each of these skills is at least slightly based on how humans perform them.** Many people say AI is a purely technical innovation that appeared out of nowhere. That view is mistaken, because AI grew out of ideas about human and animal psychology. Each part of an AI system can be traced back to a human skill it was built to imitate.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure

teaching.text: **How AI knows something connects to a 1953 paper by Wilson Taylor.** The paper is titled "Cloze Procedure," with the subtitle A New Tool for Measuring Readability. It appeared in the Fall 1953 issue of **Journalism Quarterly**, a journal devoted to research in mass communication.
children: The paper was the first full statement of a method and its theory. It reported **three pilot studies and two experiments**. In them, cloze results were compared with two existing **readability formulas**, which are formulas that estimate how easy a piece of writing is to read.

teaching.text: **Taylor's question was whether people's ability to restore deleted parts of a message could measure how readable that message was.** A tool built to measure human understanding of language ended up describing what it means for a system to know something.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern

teaching.text: **Taylor described cloze procedure as a new psychological tool for measuring the effectiveness of communication.** The method is straightforward, and the data are easily turned into numbers. The findings held up in testing.
children: At first the tool was treated as a new approach to **readability**. Its results repeatedly agreed with the **Flesch** and **Dale-Chall** formulas, the two standard devices for estimating readability. Then cloze procedure was tested directly against those formulas.
Taylor expected that if future research supported these results, the tool would have many uses in other fields involving communication.

teaching.text: **Taylor credited Charles Osgood and Melvin Marks, both experimental psychologists, for starting and helping with the work.** Others who advised or helped included Lee Cronbach, an educational psychologist and statistician, Dean Wilbur Schramm, Charles Swanson and George Klare, who had both written on readability, and the research associates Kalmer Stordahl and Clifford Christensen.
**At the center of the method is a unit of measurement called a cloze.** It is pronounced like the verb "close." The name comes from the word **closure**.
children: **Closure** is a term from **Gestalt psychology**, the branch of psychology that studies how we perceive whole patterns. Closure is the human tendency to **complete a familiar pattern that is not quite finished**. The standard example is a broken circle. We see it as a whole circle by filling in the gap in our minds.

The three black circles beside Taylor's text each have a wedge cut out. The wedges point inward toward a common center. Nothing in the figure is a triangle, yet a bright white triangle appears to sit on top of the circles. The visual system completes the triangle from the partial information the wedges provide.

sections.title: What successful completion requires

teaching.text: **The same principle applies to language.** A person can complete a broken circle because its shape is so familiar that it can be recognized even when much of it is missing. Given the sentence "Chickens cackle and ___ quack," almost anyone can instantly supply the word "ducks."
children: If the word a person supplies is the same as the word that was removed, that person scores **one cloze unit**.

teaching.text: **Filling that single blank requires a surprising amount of knowledge.** The sentence is a complex pattern built out of many smaller patterns.
children: A reader must know the **meanings** of all five words. A reader must know their **forms**, the patterns of letters in each word. A reader must know the meanings of **combinations** of words.

The reader must also notice that the sentence has two parallel halves. The first half pairs an animal with its sound, "chickens cackle." So the second half calls for the animal that goes with "quack." The reader guesses what the whole sentence means and then completes the pattern to fit that meaning.

teaching.text: **Taylor gave two formal definitions.** A **cloze unit** is any single successful attempt to reproduce a part deleted from a message, by deciding from the remaining context what the missing part should be. A message is any language product. **Cloze procedure** is a method of intercepting a message from a transmitter, a writer or speaker, deleting parts of it, and giving the damaged message to receivers, readers or listeners. Their attempts to make the patterns whole again produce cloze units that can be counted.
**AI shows its knowledge of something by completing, or clozing, sequences.** A system that can reliably fill in the missing parts of language has captured the patterns of that language.
children: The same test works for people. A teacher tests a student's knowledge of a skill by asking the student to complete some sequence, such as finishing a sentence or supplying the next step in a procedure.

AI takes this idea to its limit. From the AI point of view, **knowledge is nothing more than completion**. A system counts as knowing English if, given part of an English sequence, it can correctly produce what comes next. No further ingredient is required.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities

teaching.text: **GPT takes in a sequence of words and predicts what word should come next.** The words are the input. So the first question is what a word looks like to a computer.
children: To a computer, a word is simply **a bunch of random numbers**. Each word in the vocabulary gets its own set of numbers. The only requirement at the start is that **no two words share the same set**. The numbers do not need to mean anything at first.

teaching.text: **A list of numbers like this is called a vector.** The vector for one word could hold 1024 numbers. In the diagram, the words "chickens," "cackle," "and" and "ducks" are each drawn as a tall vertical bar, one vector per word. The input to GPT is a row of vectors, one for each word.

**Given "chickens cackle and ducks ___," a system that knows English produces an output vector of 10,000 numbers.** Each number is the probability that a particular word of English is the next word. The output is drawn as one long horizontal bar, with labels for a few of the words, "a," "cat," "quack" and "Zulu."
children: A system that knows English gives a high probability to "quack," since ducks are the animal that quacks. Words like "cat" and "Zulu" get very low probabilities, since they make no sense in that position.

The output does not choose a single word directly. It gives a probability for every word in the vocabulary at once. The most likely words are the best completions. So the system's knowledge of English shows up entirely in how well it fills the blank.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge

teaching.text: **The list of probabilities GPT produces is called a pdf, short for probability distribution function.** It describes how likely each possible next word is. The input vectors are called the **x's**. So the central question is how the system turns the x's into the pdf.

**GPT transforms the inputs through recognizing by computing.** It recognizes the pattern in the input words. That recognition is carried out entirely through computation. The computing is mostly just **addition, subtraction, multiplication and division**. This is the same **grade school arithmetic** used to add up a grocery bill. The difference is that GPT performs these operations an enormous number of times in a row.

**The knowledge the system uses to turn the x's into the pdf is stored in a bunch of numbers called w's, or weights.** The x's change every time a new sentence comes in. The w's stay fixed while the system is being used. The arithmetic combines the incoming x's with the stored w's, and the result is the pdf.
children: The knowledge is located **in** the weights. If the weights are changed, the system's predictions change. So its knowledge has changed.
Today's AI systems have **about a couple of trillion weights**. Every piece of knowledge the system has, including the fact that ducks quack, is spread across those trillions of numbers.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison

teaching.text: **Trillions of weights are not too many numbers to resemble human knowledge.** A person knows that chickens cackle but ducks quack. That knowledge has to be stored somewhere.
children: It is stored in the **synapses**, the connections between the **neurons** of the brain. A synapse is the point where one neuron passes a signal to another. The strength of each connection helps determine what the brain does with incoming information.

teaching.text: **The human brain has about 150 trillion synapses.** That is roughly 75 times the 2 trillion weights of today's largest AI systems. In both cases, knowledge is stored in a huge number of connection strengths rather than in a list of written facts. The weights play the role that synapses play in the brain.

sections.title: Completion is a form of prediction

teaching.text: **The claim that knowledge is completion strikes many people as nonsensical.** Among them is **Yann LeCun**, a leading AI researcher. He argues that this view does not make sense, and he raised **a billion dollars** on the basis of that position.

**Anyone who has used an AI system can judge the question directly.** What matters is whether the system feels like one whose notion of knowledge is **totally different** from our own. One reasonable answer is that it is **not totally different** from ours. Its answers, completions and explanations are close enough to human knowledge that the two cannot be entirely separate.

**Another term for completion is prediction, and that word sits better with people.** Humans constantly **predict** and **expect** what will happen next. It might be the next word in a sentence, the next note in a song, or the next event in a situation. So knowledge as completion is knowledge as prediction, which human minds do all the time.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

teaching.text: **AI learns by making mistakes, and humans may not be that different.** How AI learns is one of the most central issues in AI.
children: The cartoon titled "How much you learn," from the r/GetMotivated page on Reddit, has three stacks of books. The stack labeled **"From theory"** is the shortest. The stack labeled **"From practice"** is taller. The stack labeled **"From mistakes"** is by far the tallest. People learn the most from their mistakes, which matches the way AI systems learn.

teaching.text: **The main learning algorithm in AI is called Stochastic Gradient Descent, or SGD.** It sounds intimidating, but it can be understood through a very easy example, **averaging**.

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning

teaching.text: **Computing an average in the ordinary way is simple.** The average of 10, 12 and 14 is found by adding the numbers and dividing by how many there are. The sum is 36, and 36 divided by 3 is 12.

**This direct method does not work for the complex things AI deals with.** Those things include speech, language, biological molecules and scenes. For them, no simple formula can be applied once to get the answer. So a different approach is needed.

**The averaging method used in AI works in a way that extends to those complex cases.** Start with a list of numbers. Make a **wild guess**, called x, about their average. Then improve x through exposure to the data. Take one number from the list. Compare it to the current value of x. Move x **a bit closer** to that number. Repeat with another number, and then another.
children: This is **observation-based error learning**. The estimate starts out wrong. Each observation reveals how wrong it is. The estimate is corrected a little each time.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent

teaching.text: **The goal is to find the average, the essence, of the list [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72].** The average is a single number that best represents all the values. Added up, the numbers give 642, and 642 divided by 8 is 80.25. SGD reaches an estimate close to this value without ever doing that full calculation.
**SGD reaches the average in five repeated steps.**
children: First, pick any random number x as the estimate of the average. This is time 0, so the estimate is written x[0]. Suppose the number picked is 130. The guess is deliberately far from the true value.
Second, randomly pick a number d from the data. The data point reveals how far the data is from the estimate. Suppose the number picked is 98, so d[0] is 98.
Third, measure the size of the mistake. The mistake is called the **Loss**. It is the difference between the current estimate and the observed data point. Here it is 130 minus 98, which is 32.
Fourth, improve the estimate by subtracting a small part of the Loss from it. Here that small part is 10 percent of the Loss, which is 3.2. So x[1] is 130 minus 3.2, which is 126.8.
Fifth, repeat the whole cycle. Pick another number d from the data and use it the same way to improve x[1] into x[2], then x[2] into x[3], and so on.

teaching.text: **The same rule works when the estimate starts too low.** Suppose the estimate were 10 and the data point drawn were 78. The Loss would be 10 minus 78, which is negative 68. Subtracting 10 percent of a negative number means adding. So the estimate rises by 6.8, from 10 to 16.8. The estimate is always pushed toward the data, whichever side it starts on.
**The whole algorithm does two things.** It makes an initial estimate or guess. Then it uses data to improve that estimate.
children: **Stochastic** means **random**, since each data point is picked at random from the list. **Gradient** refers to the **Loss**, since the size and direction of each correction depend on how large the mistake is and which way it points. **Descent** means **reducing**, since each step reduces the mistake by moving the estimate closer to the data.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability

teaching.text: **The fraction of the Loss subtracted at each step is called the learning rate.** In the example it was 10 percent. The four graphs apply SGD to the same list with four learning rates, 10 percent, 50 percent, 1 percent and 80 percent.
children: In every graph, the vertical axis is the estimate x, from 0 to 140. The horizontal axis is **epochs**, from 0 to 300. Each epoch is one update step. Each graph has three runs from three **initial conditions (IC)**, three different starting guesses. The red run starts at 130, the green run at 80, and the blue run at 10.

teaching.text: **With a learning rate of 10 percent, the red run drops steeply from 130 and the blue run climbs steeply from 10.** Both reach the neighborhood of 80 within roughly the first 25 to 50 epochs. The green run starts near 80 and stays there. After that, all three runs overlap and wobble slightly around 80.

**With a learning rate of 1 percent, all three runs are smooth, with almost no wobble, but learning is very slow.** After 300 epochs, the red run has only come down to about 82. The blue run has only climbed to about 76. So neither has fully reached the average.

**With a learning rate of 50 percent, the red and blue runs jump to the neighborhood of 80 within the first few epochs, so learning is very fast.** Afterward, all three runs **bounce up and down widely**, roughly between 70 and 95, and never settle. **With 80 percent, the runs arrive even faster, but the bouncing is even larger**, roughly between 65 and 97.

**The bouncing comes from the random single data points used at each step.** Each update pulls the estimate toward just one number from the list. Those numbers range from 67 to 98. With a small learning rate, each pull moves the estimate only slightly, so the pulls toward high and low values average out. With a large learning rate, each pull moves the estimate most of the way toward whichever number was drawn. At 80 percent, if the estimate is 80 and the number drawn is 98, the estimate jumps by 80 percent of the 18-point gap, which is 14.4, landing at 94.4. The next draw may throw it far back down.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff

teaching.text: **The four graphs reveal the fundamental learning tradeoff.** The learning rate is written with the Greek letter γ (gamma).
children: When γ is **increased**, learning **speed increases**. The estimate reaches the neighborhood of the answer in just a few steps. At the same time, **accuracy decreases**. The estimate keeps jumping around instead of settling close to the true average.

When γ is **decreased**, learning **speed decreases**. The estimate creeps toward the answer and may still be far from it after hundreds of steps. At the same time, **accuracy increases**. The estimate moves smoothly and stays close to the true value once it gets there.

teaching.text: **Speed and accuracy pull against each other.** So a single learning rate cannot make both as good as possible at once. The 10 percent rate sits between the extremes. It reaches the average fairly quickly while wobbling only a little.

**For generations, thousands of people have made their living by finding better ways to optimize learning.** Optimizing means adjusting how learning is carried out so that **speed and accuracy both increase** at the same time. This gets around the tradeoff that a single fixed learning rate cannot escape.

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
Elements, relations, and a goal

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a system whose state changes over time according to rules.** Dynamical systems appear in two places in this course. One is **animal behavior**, such as an octopus defending its home or a person speaking. The other is **AI learning**, where a program changes its internal numbers as it is trained.

**Every dynamical system can be described with three parts, elements, relations and a goal.** The **elements** are the pieces that make up the system. The **relations** are the ways those pieces are connected and coordinated. The **goal** is what the whole coordinated system is working to achieve.
children: These three parts let very different systems be described in the same terms. The system can be an animal's body, a vocal tract or a machine learning program.

sections.title: An octopus coordinates its body with its environment

teaching.text: **An octopus defending its den is a dynamical system in behavior.** Its **elements** are its eight **arms** and the **ground** it sits on and pushes against.

**Its relations are the coordinated connections between each arm, the ground and the fish.** These relations are **planned by a neural system**. That system lives in the octopus's head and also throughout the rest of its body. So the octopus does not control its arms from one central point alone.
**Its goal is to keep the den.** The octopus coordinates its arms, its grip on the ground and the movement of the fish so that it can protect its home.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system

teaching.text: **Human speech is also a dynamical system, and it has many more elements than the octopus.** The **elements** are the **many parts of the tongue**, the **lips**, the **velum**, the **larynx**, the **palate** and the **pharyngeal wall**.
children: The tongue is not one single element. Its tip, body and root can each move somewhat independently, so it counts as many parts.

The **velum** is the soft back part of the roof of the mouth. It raises to close off the nasal passage or lowers to let air flow through the nose. The **larynx** is the voice box in the throat, which holds the vocal folds. The **palate** is the hard roof of the mouth. The **pharyngeal wall** is the back wall of the throat behind the tongue.

teaching.text: **The relations between all these parts are planned by the brain.** Producing a single word requires the lips, tongue, velum and larynx to move at precisely coordinated times.
**The goal of the speech system is to convey a thought.** All of this coordinated movement exists so that an idea in one person's mind can reach another person.
children: The real-time MRI recording shows the system in action. Over about three seconds of speech, the lips, jaw and tongue change shape and position continuously. So speech is many parts moving together over time, not a series of frozen positions.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems

teaching.text: **All daily voluntary actions, such as walking or reaching, are dynamical systems.** The involuntary actions of the heart, the pancreas and neurons are dynamical systems too. Each involves parts whose activity changes over time in coordinated ways.
children: The elements can be as big as **organs** or parts of organs. They can be as small as **cells** and the **chemicals** inside cells. So **biology, chemistry and physics** all study dynamical systems.
The **speech system** is a **very complex dynamical system**. It combines many body parts, many muscles and brain planning, all working toward one goal.

teaching.text: **There are so many dynamical systems in nature that one can be used to study another.** An octopus arm and a human tongue are extremely different on the surface. Yet they share an **underlying similarity** in how their elements, relations and goals are organized.
children: This is **going up Diotima's ladder**. Studying many different dynamical systems moves understanding from individual cases toward the general principles they all share.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action

teaching.text: **The octopus example comes from a 2023 paper in Marine Biology by Jean Alupay, Jennifer Mather and Khalil Iskarous.** The paper is titled "A syntactic analysis of a complex motor action" and is about the octopus arm slap. The researchers studied an octopus of the genus **Abdopus**, filmed in **tidal pools in Okinawa, Japan**, as it **slapped at fish** in the wild. A slap is a quick arm strike against a fish near the den. In total, 19 slaps were analyzed.
children: The arm movements were measured in two **reference frames**. An **external reference frame** measures position relative to the surroundings. An **animal-centered reference frame** measures position relative to the octopus's own body.

teaching.text: **The octopus built each slap out of two kinematic primitives, rotation and translation of its hydrostatic arms.** Kinematic primitives are basic building-block movements. Rotation means turning the arm around a point. Translation means moving the arm from one place to another without turning it.
children: A **muscular hydrostat** is a body structure with no bones. It is supported by muscles pushing against each other around an incompressible core. The octopus arm is one, so it can bend at any point along its length.
The octopus combined these primitives **serially**, one after another, and **in parallel**, at the same time.

teaching.text: **Combining a small number of primitives keeps the movement flexible while controlling only a few degrees of freedom.** A **degree of freedom** is one independent way a system can move. An octopus arm could bend in almost unlimited ways. Limiting control to a few combined primitives makes the movement manageable. The authors named this **flexible rigidity**.

**The slap supports Flash and Hochner's embodied organization view of motor behavior.** Embodied organization means that much of the organization of movement comes from the structure of the body itself, not only from commands in the brain. The slap also supports their idea that **motor primitives combine syntactically**.
children: **Syntax** in language is the set of rules for combining words into sentences. Calling the slap **syntactic** means small movement units are combined by rules into a larger action, the way words are combined into sentences. So one dynamical system, the octopus arm, is used to study another, human language.

teaching.text: **The octopus uses sensory feedback about the moving fish together with feed-forward motor primitives.** **Feedback** is information from the senses during the movement that allows correction. **Feed-forward** control sends out a pre-planned movement without waiting for correction. Together they let the octopus stay in **dynamic equilibrium** with a changing environment.
children: The paper's keywords are **Octopus, Muscular hydrostat, Motor control** and **Abdopus**. The book Octopus, The Ocean's Intelligent Invertebrate, by Jennifer Mather, Roland Anderson and James Wood, is a broader source on octopus behavior.

sections.title: Knowledge and other psychological skills in AI

teaching.text: **AI is a model of five animal psychological skills, knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning.** It is a system built to imitate abilities that animals, including humans, already have.
children: **Knowing** is holding stored information about the world, such as how words are used. **Recognizing** is identifying what something is when it is encountered. **Attending** is focusing on the parts of the input that matter most. **Acting** is producing an output, such as a movement for an animal or a word for a language model. **Learning** is changing internal knowledge based on experience so that future performance improves.

teaching.text: **The cloze procedure is an early example of measuring one of these skills in humans.** Wilson Taylor introduced it in "Cloze Procedure," subtitled A New Tool for Measuring Readability, in Journalism Quarterly in Fall 1953.
children: In a **cloze task**, words are removed from a passage and readers fill in the blanks. The more easily readers guess the missing words, the more readable and predictable the text is. The article reported three pilot studies and two experiments comparing cloze results with two readability formulas.
Filling in a missing word from its context is the same basic skill that modern language AI performs. It predicts a word from the words around it.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution

teaching.text: **In GPT, each word is represented as a vector, a list of thousands of numbers.** These vectors are called **x's** or **tokens**. In "chickens cackle and ducks," each of the four words is its own tall column of numbers, one column per token.

**All of the AI's knowledge is stored in a few trillion numbers called weights, or w's.** The weights are not a dictionary or a list of facts. They are numbers whose values together determine how the system responds to input.

**The AI combines the W's with the x's using mostly addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.** The complexity comes from the enormous number of these simple calculations. No single operation is complicated.

**These calculations produce a probability distribution function over possible next words.** A **probability distribution** gives each possible word a probability, and all the probabilities add up to one. The distribution is the system's way of saying "this is my guess for the next word."
children: For "chickens cackle and ducks," the curve has small bumps over many words and a tallest peak over **"quack."** Words like "a," "cat" and "Zulu" get only a little probability.

teaching.text: **The way the W's combine with the x's is itself a dynamical system.** Learning is a simpler dynamical system than this prediction process. So learning is the easier one to work through first.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful

teaching.text: **The weights come from a training process that starts with no knowledge at all.** The approach is summed up as "Fake it till you make it!" Training repeats a sequence of steps.
children: The system **starts with random W's**. Any values at all can be used as the starting point.
The system is given a sequence of words, such as "chickens cackle and ducks." It is asked to **predict the next word** by combining its W's with the input vectors.
With random weights, the prediction is poor. The tallest peak might sit over "cat," with only low, uneven probability on the other words, including "quack."

We already know the correct next word is "quack." The **target distribution** puts all of the probability on "quack" as a single sharp spike and zero on every other word. The system is told to **change its W's** so that its output looks more like this target.
The system is exposed to **more sequences** and asked to predict again, **billions of times**. Each time its W's are changed to **improve its guessing**.

teaching.text: **This repeated cycle of guessing, comparing and adjusting is how LLMs learn and know.** A large language model gets all of its knowledge from gradually correcting random weights over billions of examples.

sections.title: Random initialization and learning from mistakes

teaching.text: **AI learning depends on two tricks, each captured by a phrase in an image generated by ChatGPT.**
children: The first trick is **"Fake It Till You Make It."** The system begins with **random weights** and makes predictions right away. Those first predictions are essentially meaningless. The system does not wait until it has knowledge before acting. It acts first and gains knowledge along the way.

The second trick is **"Learn by Making Mistakes."** Each wrong prediction produces an **error**, the difference between what the system guessed and what was correct. The system uses that error to adjust its weights. So every mistake becomes information that improves the next prediction.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average

teaching.text: **Finding an average seems very easy with a short list of numbers.** The average of 10, 12 and 14 is found by adding them and dividing by how many there are. The sum is 36, and 36 divided by 3 gives 12.

**This simple formula does not work for complex things like speech, language, biological molecules and scenes.** Those are exactly what AI works with. For them, there is no short list of numbers to add up and divide. So a method that improves an estimate step by step is needed.

**The averaging method used here learns from the data one piece at a time.** Start with a **list of numbers**. Make a **wild guess**, called x, about their average. Take one number from the list and check how far it is from x. Move x **a bit closer** to that number. Repeat with another number, and then another.
children: This is **observation-based error learning**. Each observation reveals an error in the current guess. The guess is corrected in the direction of that observation.

This is the same logic as training an LLM, applied to a much simpler problem. The random starting guess for x plays the role of the random starting weights. Moving x toward each observed number plays the role of changing the weights toward the correct next word.

sections.title: Start from an arbitrary estimate

teaching.text: **SGD, stochastic gradient descent, estimates an average by learning from the data one observation at a time.** The list is [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72]. Its true average, its **essence**, is 80.25, found by adding the eight numbers to get 642 and dividing by eight. That is the target the learning process should approach.

**SGD does not start by calculating that average. It starts by picking any random number x as the estimate.** At **time 0**, the estimate is set to 130, which is far above every number in the list. So x[0] is 130.
children: The number in brackets is the **time step**. The value x[0] is the estimate at time 0. The value x[1] is the estimate after one update, and so on.

teaching.text: **The learning rate, written γ, is set to 25 percent.** The learning rate controls how large each correction is. It is the fraction of the error that the estimate moves on each step.
children: Plotted against the update number, the estimate at time 0 is a single point at 130. The true average of 80.25 sits far below it as a flat horizontal line.

sections.title: An observation exposes a discrepancy

teaching.text: **The first step of learning is to randomly pick one number d from the data.** The first observation drawn is 98. So d[0] is 98.

**The discrepancy, also called the loss, is the difference between the current estimate and the observation.** The estimate is 130 and the observation is 98. So the loss is 32. The loss measures how wrong the estimate is compared with this piece of data.
children: The discrepancy is positive, so the estimate is 32 units too high compared with this observation. The average should be **close to the data**. So an estimate far from an observed value needs to change.
Plotted together at update 0, the estimate is at 130 and the observation is at 98, below it. The true average of 80.25 is lower still.

sections.title: Correct a fraction rather than replacing the guess

teaching.text: **The correction step subtracts 25 percent of the discrepancy from the current estimate.** The discrepancy is 32 and the learning rate is 0.25. So the correction is 8. Subtracting 8 from 130 gives the new estimate. So x[1] is 122.

**The estimate moves toward this observation, but not all the way.** It moves one quarter of the distance, from 130 to 122. Moving only part of the way keeps any single observation from taking over the estimate.
children: Plotted over updates, the estimate line drops from 130 at update 0 to 122 at update 1. It is heading down toward the average line at 80.25.

sections.title: Correction after observation 2

teaching.text: **The same procedure repeats with a new random observation each time.** Draw a number. Compute the discrepancy. Subtract 25 percent of that discrepancy from the estimate.

**On the second update, the random observation is 85.** The current estimate is 122. The discrepancy is 37. The correction is 25 percent of 37, which is 9.25. Subtracting it gives 112.75. So x[2] is 112.75, and the estimate moved toward the observation.

sections.title: Correction after observation 3

teaching.text: **On the third update, the random observation is 76.** The estimate of 112.75 is still above the observation, so the discrepancy is positive. The discrepancy is 36.75. The correction is 25 percent of 36.75, which is 9.1875. Subtracting it gives about 103.563. So x[3] is about 103.563.

sections.title: Correction after observation 4

teaching.text: **On the fourth update, the random observation is 68.** The discrepancy between 103.563 and 68 is 35.563. The correction is 25 percent of that, about 8.891. Subtracting it gives 94.672. So x[4] is 94.672.

**Across the first four updates, the estimate falls steadily.** It went 130, 122, 112.75, 103.563 and 94.672. Every observation so far has been below the estimate. So every correction has pushed the estimate down toward the average line at 80.25.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: **On the fifth update, the random observation is 98, which is higher than the current estimate of 94.672.** A **datum** is a single data point. The discrepancy is now **negative**, because the estimate is below the observation. It is 94.672 minus 98, which is negative 3.328.

**The rule still says to subtract 25 percent of the discrepancy.** The correction is a negative number, about negative 0.832. Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding. So a negative discrepancy makes the subtraction **move x upward**. The estimate rises slightly from 94.672 to 95.504, toward the high observation.
children: The same single rule handles both cases. When the estimate is above an observation, the discrepancy is positive and the estimate goes down. When the estimate is below an observation, the discrepancy is negative and the estimate goes up. In both cases the estimate moves toward the observation.
Plotted over updates, the estimate line bends slightly upward at update 5 after four straight drops. This is the first sign that the path does not move smoothly in one direction.

sections.title: Correction after observation 6

teaching.text: **On the sixth update, the random observation is 72, which is below the estimate again.** The discrepancy between 95.504 and 72 is 23.504. The correction is 25 percent of that, which is 5.876. Subtracting it gives 89.628. So x[6] is 89.628.

sections.title: Correction after observation 7

teaching.text: **On the seventh update, the random observation is 78.** The discrepancy between 89.628 and 78 is 11.628. It is smaller than before because the estimate is now much closer to the data. The correction is 25 percent of 11.628, which is 2.907. Subtracting it gives 86.721. So x[7] is 86.721.

sections.title: Correction after observation 8

teaching.text: **On the eighth update, the random observation is 67, the lowest number in the list.** The discrepancy between 86.721 and 67 is 19.721. The correction is 25 percent of that, about 4.930. Subtracting it gives 81.791. So x[8] is 81.791.
**After eight updates, the estimate is only about 1.5 above the true average of 80.25.**

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: **On the ninth update, the random observation is 98 once more.** The value 98 appears twice in the list. Each draw is random, so the same value can be picked more than once. This is the third time 98 has been drawn.

**The estimate of 81.791 is well below 98, so the discrepancy is negative and fairly large, negative 16.209.** Subtracting 25 percent of a negative discrepancy, about negative 4.052, moves the estimate upward. It goes from 81.791 to 85.843.
children: A single high observation pushed the estimate away from the true average, even though the estimate had been getting very close. Each step responds only to the one observation drawn, not to the whole data set.

sections.title: Correction after observation 10

teaching.text: **On the tenth update, the random observation is 85, which is extremely close to the current estimate.** The discrepancy between 85.843 and 85 is 0.843, which is less than 1. So the correction is tiny, about 0.211. The estimate barely moves, from 85.843 to 85.632.
children: When an observation agrees closely with the estimate, the estimate hardly changes. The path is almost level between updates 9 and 10.

sections.title: Correction after observation 11

teaching.text: **On the eleventh update, the random observation is 76.** The discrepancy between 85.632 and 76 is 9.632. The correction is 25 percent of that, which is 2.408. Subtracting it gives 83.224. So x[11] is 83.224.

sections.title: Correction after observation 12

teaching.text: **On the twelfth update, the random observation is 68.** The discrepancy between 83.224 and 68 is 15.224. The correction is 25 percent of that, which is 3.806. Subtracting it gives 79.418. So x[12] is 79.418. This is less than 1 below the true average of 80.25, even though the process started at 130.

**Over all twelve updates, the estimate went 130, 122, 112.75, 103.563, 94.672, 95.504, 89.628, 86.721, 81.791, 85.843, 85.632, 83.224 and 79.418.** The path falls steeply at first. It bumps upward twice when 98 is drawn. It ends up hovering near the average line.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters

teaching.text: **SGD consists of two steps.** First, **make an initial estimate or guess**, which can be completely random. Second, **use data to improve the estimate**, one observation at a time, by moving the estimate part of the way toward each observation.
**Each word in the name describes part of the method.**
children: **Stochastic** means a **random observation** is used. At each step, the data point for the correction is picked at random. This is why the estimate is sometimes pushed down and sometimes pulled up.

**Gradient** means a **loss-related direction**. The discrepancy tells how wrong the estimate is and which way it needs to move. A positive discrepancy means move down. A negative discrepancy means move up.
**Descent** means **reducing the mistake**. Every correction makes the error for the observed data point smaller.

teaching.text: **The path jitters, but its tendency is toward the average.** Individual steps can move away from the true average, as happened when 98 was drawn. Over many updates, the random pushes up and down balance out, and the estimate settles near 80.
children: This is observation-based error learning in its simplest form. The same method, applied to trillions of weights instead of a single number x, is how LLMs change their W's to predict the next word.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls

teaching.text: **A second data set makes the relationship between the estimate and the loss easier to track.** The data are [62, 70, 78, 82, 90, 98]. They add up to 480, and 480 divided by 6 is 80. So the average is 80.

**The mean motion of SGD describes how the estimate moves on average.** Each random observation is sometimes above and sometimes below the average. So on average the estimate is pulled toward the mean of the data, 80. Replacing the random observation with the average gives the rule for the mean motion. The new estimate x[t plus 1] equals the old estimate x[t] minus 25 percent of the distance between the old estimate and 80.
children: Here t stands for any time step. So this one rule describes every update.

teaching.text: **The loss at each time step is one half of the discrepancy squared.** Squaring makes the loss positive whether the estimate is too high or too low. So both kinds of mistake count as error. The loss is zero only when the estimate equals 80 exactly.
children: The rate at which this loss changes as x changes equals the discrepancy, x[t] minus 80. This is why the discrepancy is the **gradient**, the loss-related direction. Subtracting a fraction of it moves the estimate in the direction that lowers the loss.

teaching.text: **The starting point is set far above the average, at x[0] equal to 140.** At time 0, the discrepancy is 60. So the loss is one half of 3600, which is 1800. On the first update, the estimate moves 25 percent of the way toward 80, from 140 to 125. The loss falls to one half of 2025, which is 1012.5. On the second update, the estimate falls to 113.75, and the loss falls to about 569.5.
children: Each update keeps 75 percent of the previous discrepancy. So the discrepancy shrinks from 60 to 45 to 33.75 and keeps shrinking. The estimate curve falls quickly at first and then flattens as it approaches the target line at 80. It reaches about 82 by update 12. The loss curve falls from 1800 at update 0 to nearly 0 by update 12.

The mean motion is **smooth** with no jitter, unlike the stochastic path. This is because it uses the average of the data instead of a random observation at each step. In this case, the **estimate goes down and the loss goes down** together.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls

teaching.text: **The same data set and the same learning rate of 25 percent can be used with only the initial condition changed.** The **initial condition** is the starting value of the estimate. This time the estimate starts far below the average, at x[0] equal to negative 100.
children: At time 0, the discrepancy is negative 180. Squaring makes the loss positive and very large. It is one half of 32400, which is 16200.

teaching.text: **On the first update, subtracting 25 percent of a negative discrepancy moves the estimate upward.** The estimate goes from negative 100 to negative 55. The loss falls to 9112.5. On the second update, the estimate rises again, to negative 21.25. The loss falls to about 5125.8.

**The estimate rises toward 80.** It climbs from negative 100 to about 74 by update 12. The discrepancy shrinks in size at every step. So one half of the discrepancy squared falls toward 0, from 16200 at update 0 to nearly 0 by update 12.

**The direction changes, but the learning does not.** Starting above the average, the estimate moves down. Starting below the average, the estimate moves up. In both cases the loss decreases. So learning is defined by the loss going down, not by the estimate moving in any particular direction.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition

teaching.text: **SGD can be run for 300 epochs, meaning 300 update steps, with three initial conditions and four learning rates.** The three initial conditions are IC of 130, well above the average, IC of 80, right at the average, and IC of 10, well below it. Every run settles around 80, the average of the data.
children: With a **learning rate of 10 percent**, the run starting at 130 falls and the run starting at 10 rises. Both reach the neighborhood of 80 within about the first 25 to 50 epochs. After that, all three runs wiggle gently within a few units of 80, roughly between 75 and 85.

With a **learning rate of 50 percent**, the runs starting at 130 and 10 reach the neighborhood of 80 within the first few epochs. After that, all three runs jump up and down widely, roughly between 70 and 95. They never settle.

With a **learning rate of 1 percent**, the runs move very slowly and very smoothly. After 300 epochs, the run starting at 130 has only come down to about 82. The run starting at 10 has only climbed to about 77. So neither has fully reached the average.

With a **learning rate of 80 percent**, the runs reach the average region almost immediately. After that, all three runs jump violently, roughly between 68 and 98, which is nearly the full range of the data. Each update moves the estimate most of the way to whatever observation was just drawn. So the estimate mostly tracks individual data points instead of their average.

teaching.text: **The initial condition affects only the first part of each run.** After enough epochs, all three runs behave the same way. The learning rate determines how fast they arrive and how much they jitter once they get there.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff

teaching.text: **The learning rate creates a fundamental learning tradeoff between speed and accuracy.**
children: When γ **increases**, learning **speed increases**. Each correction is larger, so the estimate reaches the average region in fewer steps. At the same time, **accuracy decreases**. The large corrections make the estimate jump around the average instead of settling on it.

When γ **decreases**, learning **speed decreases**. Each correction is small, so the estimate needs many steps to reach the average. At the same time, **accuracy increases**. The small corrections keep the estimate steady and close to the true average once it arrives.

teaching.text: **With a single learning rate, the fastest learning and the most accurate result cannot be had at the same time.** The 1 percent run is accurate but slow. The 50 and 80 percent runs are fast but noisy.

**Thousands of people, for generations, have made their living finding better ways to optimize.** To optimize means to adjust a learning process so that it works as well as possible. The goal is to find methods where **speed increases and accuracy increases** together. Then systems like LLMs can learn quickly while ending up with accurate weights.

lecture04.title: 04 · Dynamic programming and shared physical principles

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem

teaching.text: **The shortest path problem asks for the cheapest route through a network, from a start to an end.** Each point is a **state**, a place we can be at a given moment. Each arrow is a possible move from one state to another. Each arrow carries a number called its **cost**. The cost can stand for distance, time, effort or anything to be kept as small as possible. The total cost of a route is the sum of the costs on every arrow along it.

**The network starts at A and ends at J, and the states sit in columns called stages.** Every arrow moves forward exactly one stage. Stage one holds A. Stage two holds B and C. Stage three holds D, E and F. Stage four holds G, H and I. Stage five holds J. So any route from A to J crosses exactly four arrows and makes exactly four decisions.
children: From A, the arrow to B costs 12 and the arrow to C costs 7. From B, the arrows to D, E and F cost 5, 6 and 9. From C, the arrows to D, E and F cost 14, 10 and 11.

From D, the arrows to G, H and I cost 8, 7 and 10. From E they cost 9, 7 and 9. From F they cost 10, 7 and 8. The last stage has one arrow out of each state. G to J costs 5, H to J costs 9, and I to J costs 8.

teaching.text: **This network is a model of decision-making over time.** Every choice has an immediate cost. Every choice also controls which states, and so which future costs, are available at the next stage. A choice that looks good now can lock us into expensive moves later.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose

teaching.text: **A greedy algorithm takes the cheapest arrow out of the current state and never looks further ahead than one move.**
children: At A, the choices are 12 to B and 7 to C, so greed goes to **C**. At C, the choices are 14, 10 and 11, so greed goes to **E**. At E, the choices are 9, 7 and 9, so greed goes to **H**. At H there is only one arrow, to J, and it costs 9.
The greedy route A, C, E, H, J costs 7 plus 10 plus 7 plus 9, which is 33. The route A, B, D, G, J starts with the more expensive move of 12. Its total is 12 plus 5 plus 8 plus 5, which is 30.

teaching.text: **Greed is not good for this problem.** The greedy rule failed at the very first decision. The cheap move to C led into a part of the network where every continuation was more costly. Greed also walked straight into H, which ends with the large final cost of 9. The greedy algorithm has no way of knowing about costs that come later. So a late obstacle can make an early cheap-looking choice a bad one.

**A very small network makes the failure of greed easy to see.** From a start there are two routes to an end, each through one middle state. On the top route, the first arrow costs 10 and the second costs 10. On the bottom route, the first arrow costs only 2, but the second costs 100.
children: A greedy decision at the start compares 10 with 2 and picks the bottom route. Then it gets stuck paying 100. The totals are 20 for the top route and 102 for the bottom route. So the top route is five times cheaper, even though its first step was five times more expensive.

Write inside each middle state the cost of getting from that state to the end, 10 on top and 100 on the bottom. Now the decision at the start is simple. Add the cost of the first arrow to the number stored in the state it leads to, and compare 20 with 102. Storing the cost of the rest of the journey inside each state removes the blindness of greed.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: **An exhaustive algorithm solves the shortest path problem by brute force.** It lists every possible route from start to end. It adds up the cost of each one. It picks the smallest total. Nothing is skipped, so the answer is **guaranteed to be correct**.
children: The number of routes comes from multiplying the number of choices at each stage. From A there are 2 choices. From the second stage there are 3. From the third stage there are 3. From the fourth stage there is only 1. So there are 18 complete routes. Each needs 3 additions to total, so checking every route takes 54 additions, followed by comparing 18 totals.

teaching.text: **The problem with exhaustive search is its growth.** Every added stage multiplies the number of routes by the number of choices at that stage. Every added state per stage makes each multiplier larger. With **many stages and many states**, the number of routes explodes. Checking all of them takes a very, very long time.
children: Exhaustive search is accurate but impractical for large problems. Greedy search is fast but can be wrong. A method is needed that is both accurate and efficient.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: **Bellman approached the problem by starting with an imaginary step.** Imagine we already knew the best possible cost of getting from B to J, and from C to J. These numbers are called VBJ and VCJ. The letter V stands for **Value**. The Value of a state is the lowest total cost of getting from that state to the goal.

**If those two Values were known, the best cost from A to J, VAJ, would follow from one short calculation.** Any route out of A goes first to either B or C, because those are the only two arrows leaving A.
children: Going to B costs 12 for that arrow. Then the best possible rest of the trip is VBJ. So the best total through B is 12 plus VBJ. Going to C costs 7, and then the best rest of the trip is VCJ. So the best total through C is 7 plus VCJ. The best cost from A is whichever of these two totals is smaller.

The word **min** means take the minimum, the smallest number in the set inside the braces. Each number in the set is built the same way. It is the cost of one arrow plus the Value of the state that arrow leads to.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: **The difficulty is that we do not know VBJ or VCJ.** The rule for VAJ is correct. But it depends on two numbers that have not yet been found.

**Bellman's general strategy handles exactly this situation. To solve a problem, decompose it into subproblems you can solve.** Finding VAJ becomes two smaller problems, finding VBJ and finding VCJ. The phrase "if you can" matters. If a subproblem still cannot be solved directly, it gets broken down again into even smaller subproblems.
