**Adding mass lowers the frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves.** How much the mass moves depends on where the mass is.
**Where there is the most movement there is no stretching, and where there is the most stretching there is no movement.**
**Adding stiffness raises the frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses.** This also depends on where the spring is.
In a **fixed-fixed system**, the harmonics are **whole-number multiples of the base frequency**, because the first mode fits a whole number of times into each mode.
In a **fixed-free system**, the frequencies are **odd multiples of the base frequency**, because the first mode fits an odd number of times into each mode.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: **Making one spot on a string heavier lowers some modes and leaves others the same.** Suppose the very middle of the string is made thicker, which adds mass there.
children: In **Mode 1**, the middle moves up and down a lot, so the added mass **lowers** the frequency.
In **Mode 2**, the middle does not move, so the added mass changes **nothing**.
In **Mode 3**, the middle moves again, so the frequency drops. In **Mode 4**, the middle is still again, so nothing changes.
Going up through the modes, the effect **alternates** between lowering the frequency and having no effect.

teaching.text: **Movement and stretching take turns along a vibrating string.** Where a piece of string moves the most, it is carried up and down and is hardly stretched. Where the string is stretched the most, such as right next to a fixed end, there is **no movement**.
children: **The shortcut is that the most springiness is at the points with no movement.**

In **Mode 5** of a string fixed at both ends, the string does not move at the **two fixed ends** or at the **four points where it crosses its middle line**. Those **six places** have the most springiness.
The opposite question has the opposite answer. The **most movement**, and the **least springiness**, is at the tops of the **five bumps**.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently

teaching.text: **One small change to a string can make one mode lower and another mode higher.** Choose a spot where **Mode 4 moves the most** and where **Mode 5 crosses its middle line**, so Mode 5 does not move at that spot. Then raise both the **mass** and the **stiffness** of that spot.
children: **For Mode 4**, the spot is moving, so the extra mass **lowers** the frequency. The spot is barely stretched, so the extra stiffness does nothing.
**For Mode 5**, the spot does not move, so the extra mass does nothing. The spot is stretched the most, so the extra stiffness **raises** the frequency.
So the same change **lowers Mode 4 and raises Mode 5**.

teaching.text: **Each mode is checked separately with one question, which is whether the spot is moving or stretching in that mode.** If the spot is moving, the mass is what matters. If the spot is stretching, the stiffness is what matters.

**This reasoning about small local changes is called perturbation theory, and it was first tested on drums.** A drum is also made of countless masses and springs. In the late nineteenth century, before cameras could record fast motion, small amounts of **wax** were stuck onto different spots on a drum.
children: Wax on a spot predicted to vibrate a lot added moving mass, and listeners heard the drum's frequency **drop**.
Wax on a spot predicted not to move made **no difference** to the sound.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are a membrane, so they have many modes of vibration, like a drum.** The **larynx** holds the **vocal folds**. In Mode 1, the whole surface moves up and down together. In Mode 2, the two halves move against each other. Higher modes divide the surface into more and more parts.

**Changing the mass or stiffness of the vocal folds changes the voice.** People who smoke heavily can develop **nodules** on their vocal folds. A nodule adds mass at one spot and changes the stiffness nearby, so the folds vibrate differently, and the voice sounds different.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: **The measured voice matched the prediction of evenly spaced harmonics.** Science states a theory, usually with **differential equations**, solves it to get a prediction, and then measures. The theory here is that the vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once, so a voice should have a spectrum with **evenly spaced harmonics**.
children: A voice recorded and examined in **Praat** had its lowest harmonic at about 130 hertz.
The next harmonics were close to two and three times that value.
Each person's lowest frequency is different, but the harmonics above it are always close to multiples of it.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: **A building is fixed at the bottom and free at the top.** In strong wind or an earthquake, the top of a building can sway.
children: Engineers design buildings to sway in **Mode 1**, with the whole building moving together. On a high floor, Mode 1 feels unpleasant, but it is safe.
Engineers design buildings to never vibrate in a higher mode. In a higher mode, some floors would move one way and other floors the other way, which would break the building.

teaching.text: **The air inside the vocal tract is also fixed at one end and free at the other end.**
children: At the bottom, the **vocal folds are closed**, so the air there **cannot move**, and that end is **fixed**.
At the lips, the air can move in and out easily, so that end is **free**.

Unlike a building, the air in the vocal tract vibrates in **all of its modes**. Speaking changes the masses and springs of different parts of the air, and that is how listeners tell vowels, consonants and words apart.

teaching.text: **A fixed-free system has frequencies only at odd multiples, such as 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz.**
children: The first mode goes from **no motion** at the fixed end to **lots of motion** at the free end. That is one quarter of a wave.
The next possible mode holds **three** of these quarter pieces, so its frequency is three times the first. The mode after that holds **five**, so its frequency is five times the first.
Two quarter pieces would end with no motion at both ends, which is a fixed-fixed pattern. So even multiples never happen.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a chain of masses and springs that is fixed at the glottis end and free at the lip end.** In this model, the masses stand for the air's inertia, which is its resistance to being moved, and the springs stand for its springiness.
children: The lowest mode of the chain is like the **first formant**, written **F1**. The next mode is like the **second formant**, written **F2**.
The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**. The frequencies of a fixed-fixed system are called **harmonics**.
The second mode vibrates **three times faster** than the first, because the second mode holds three quarter-wave pieces.
The masses near the free end move very freely in both modes.

teaching.text: **Three places along the tube matter for vowels.**
children: **/a/** is made by squeezing the air **one third of the way from the glottis**.
**/i/** is made by squeezing the air **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
**/u/** is made by squeezing the air at the **lips**, which is the free end.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: **Images of the vocal tract show where each vowel squeezes the air.** A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips narrow the tract and squeeze the air. The **glottis** is the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end, so distances are measured from the glottis.
children: In **done**, the central vowel, there is **no constriction**, and air flows freely along the whole tract.
In **dean**, a **high front** vowel, the air is squeezed under the roof of the mouth, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, a **low back** vowel, the air is squeezed far back in the throat, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, a **high back** vowel, the lips are rounded, so the air is squeezed **at the lips**.
**Dan** is a **low front** vowel.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **Squeezing air raises both its stiffness and its mass.**
children: Squeezing air makes it **stiffer**, the same way pressing on a tire makes the tire stiffer.
Squeezing air also packs it into a smaller space, which raises its **density**. Denser air is more **massive** and harder to move.

teaching.text: **Raising mass and stiffness together does not cancel out in a system with many masses and springs.** Canceling out only happens for a single mass on a single spring.
children: In a system with many masses and springs, each spot is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching** in a given mode.
At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, only the extra stiffness counts, so the frequency **goes up**.
At a spot with lots of motion and no stretching, only the extra mass counts, so the frequency **goes down**.
Speech proves that the effects do not cancel, because constrictions in different places clearly change the frequencies of the voice.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: **For /u/, rounding the lips lowers both F1 and F2.** Rounding the lips squeezes the air at the **free end**, which raises the mass and the stiffness of the air there.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air at the free end moves a lot and hardly compresses, so **motion matters most**. The extra mass lowers **F1**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at the free end again moves a lot, so **motion matters most**. The extra mass lowers **F2**.
The extra stiffness does not matter in either mode, because the air at the lips is moving, not stretching.

teaching.text: **A recording confirmed the prediction.** A speaker started from the central vowel, with formants near 500, 1500 and 2500 hertz, and then said /u/. **Both formants dropped**, because the rounded lips added mass right where the air moves the most.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **For /i/, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** The air is squeezed about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**, and that one spot acts differently in the two modes.
children: In **Mode 1**, this spot has lots of motion and hardly any compression, so **mass matters most**. The extra mass **lowers F1**.
In **Mode 2**, this spot has lots of compression, so **springiness matters most**. The extra stiffness **raises F2**.
In plain terms, the same squeeze lands on a moving spot for F1 and on a springy spot for F2, so one formant falls while the other rises.

teaching.text: **A recording confirmed the prediction.** A speaker went from the central vowel into /i/. The **first formant dropped a lot**, and the **second formant went up**.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: **For /a/, F1 goes up and F2 goes down, which is the reverse of /i/.** The air is squeezed about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
children: In **Mode 1**, this spot near the fixed end has lots of compression, so **springiness matters most**. The extra stiffness **raises F1**.
In **Mode 2**, this spot has lots of motion, so **mass matters most**. The extra mass **lowers F2**.
So F1 and F2 move toward each other, and the two formants end up close together.

teaching.text: **The same reasoning works backward.**
children: If a constriction raises a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be **springy and hardly moving** in that mode.
If a constriction lowers a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be **moving a lot** in that mode.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: **The mass-spring principles explain every vowel.** Raising mass lowers frequency, and raising stiffness raises frequency, but each change only matters where it can act.
children: **Extra mass matters where the air moves.**
**Extra stiffness matters where the air compresses and expands.**
The vocal tract is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips, so its formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: **The air in the tube can be modeled as lines of air particles.** Each particle stands for billions of real air molecules. The closed vocal folds sit at the **fixed end**, and the open lips sit at the **free end**.
children: Where the lines bunch close together and then spread far apart, the air is **compressing and expanding**, which is called **springiness**.
Where the lines move back and forth without changing their spacing, the air is acting as a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the **free end**, where the air simply moves in and out.
At the fixed end, the air cannot move, but the air there compresses and expands a lot.

teaching.text: **The modes of the air match the modes of a building.**
children: **F1** has one point of no motion, at the fixed end.
**F2** has two points of no motion, one at the fixed end and one inside the tube.
**F3** has three points of no motion. Between them, the air takes turns between places of most motion and places of most compression.

teaching.text: **The schwa matches the prediction for a uniform tube.** The **schwa** is the central vowel with no constriction. F2 should be three times F1, and F3 should be five times F1. A measured schwa had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**, which are those odd multiples.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **A short question like "Where were you a year ago?" uses all of the constriction rules at once.** Each sound squeezes the air at a different place, so the formants move up and down the whole time.
children: When the tongue makes an **/i/**-like squeeze near the front of the mouth, **F1 goes down and F2 goes up**, because that spot moves in Mode 1 and is springy in Mode 2.
When the lips round for "you," **F1 and F2 both go down**, because the free end moves in every mode.
When the tongue moves back and down, as in an **/a/**-like sound, **F1 goes up and F2 goes down**, because that spot is springy in Mode 1 and moves in Mode 2.

teaching.text: **Speech is a continuous series of constrictions, not a list of separate vowels.** The frequencies of the air in the vocal tract are always changing, and the mass-spring rules predict which way each formant moves at every moment.

lecture13.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production · Source and Filter

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: **Every vibrating system in speech follows the same short list of principles.**
children: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.**
**A system with n masses has n modes.** Each higher mode has a higher frequency, because more parts move against each other and more springs stretch.

**Adding mass lowers the frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves.** A mass that does not move has no effect. A mass that moves a little has a small effect. A mass that moves a lot has a large effect.
**Adding stiffness raises the frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses.** Both effects depend on where the change is made.
**Where there is the most movement there is no stretching, and where there is the most stretching there is no movement.**
In a **fixed-fixed system**, the frequencies are called **harmonics**, and they are **whole-number multiples** of the base frequency.
In a **fixed-free system**, the frequencies are called **formants**, and they are **odd multiples** of the base frequency.

teaching.text: **Raising mass and stiffness at the same time does not cancel out, except for a single mass on a single spring.** In a system with many masses and springs, a spot that moves a lot hardly stretches, and a spot that stretches a lot hardly moves. So at any one spot, only one of the two changes matters.
children: Picture a spot on a string that never moves but is stretched hard. Extra mass at that spot does nothing. Extra stiffness at that spot raises the frequency. So the frequency goes up.
Picture a spot on a string that moves up and down the most. Extra stiffness at that spot does nothing. Extra mass at that spot slows it down. So the frequency goes down.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: **Adding masses adds modes, and the same mode shapes repeat.**
children: **Mode 1** always has everything moving together.
**Mode 2** always splits the system into two halves that move against each other.
**Mode 3** always has the middle moving against the sides.

teaching.text: **Higher modes are stiffer and faster because more parts move against each other.** More parts moving against each other means more springs are stretching.
children: In plain terms, a higher mode does not have stiffer springs. A higher mode makes the same springs do more stretching.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples

teaching.text: **In a string fixed at both ends, each higher mode is made of more copies of the first mode.** The first mode is **one half-wave**. A half-wave is one bump that goes from no motion at one end, to the most motion in the middle, to no motion at the other end.
children: **Mode 2 holds two half-waves.** One half goes up while the other half goes down. Each half acts like a copy of Mode 1, so Mode 2 has **twice the stiffness** and **twice the frequency**.
**Mode 3 holds three half-waves**, and **Mode 5 holds five**, so the fifth mode has five times the frequency of the first.
So the frequencies climb in equal steps. If the first harmonic is 100 hertz, the next harmonics are 200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz.

teaching.text: **The numbers do not have to start at 100.** A voice with a base frequency of **250 hertz** has its next harmonics at 500, 750 and 1000 hertz. Each harmonic is still a whole number of copies of the first.
children: The short exam answer is that **the fifth mode has the first mode fitted into it five times**, so it has five times the stiffness and five times the frequency.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: **A string fixed at both ends vibrates in all its modes at once, and its spectrum has evenly spaced spikes.** A **spectrum** has **frequency** along the bottom and **amplitude**, or strength, going up. Each spike is one harmonic.
children: The **vocal folds** are fixed on all sides, just behind the Adam's apple. So the vocal folds behave like this kind of fixed-fixed system and produce harmonics.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: **The same copy-counting works on a membrane.** The vocal folds form a **membrane**, which is a vibrating sheet.
children: The first mode is one bump across the whole membrane.
The second mode fits two of those bumps, so it has twice the frequency.
The fourth mode fits four ups and downs, so it has four times the frequency.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: **A building is fixed at the bottom and free at the top.** In strong wind or an earthquake, engineers want a building to sway only in **Mode 1**, with the whole building moving together.
children: Mode 1 feels unpleasant on a high floor, but it is safe.
A higher mode would send some floors one way and other floors the other way, and the building could break apart.

teaching.text: **A string can also be fixed at the bottom and free at the top.** The first mode of this string is not a full half-wave. The first mode goes from **no motion at the fixed end** to **the most motion at the free end**, which is only **one quarter of a wave**.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples

teaching.text: **In a fixed-free system, each mode is built from quarter-wave pieces.** Each piece goes from no motion to the most motion.
children: **Mode 1 holds one piece.**
**Mode 2 holds three pieces.**
**Mode 3 holds five pieces.**
**Mode 4 holds seven pieces.**
So with a base of 100 hertz, the modes come at 100, 300, 500 and 700 hertz.

teaching.text: **Two pieces can never fit, so the steps are always odd.**
children: First, two pieces stacked together give no motion, then the most motion, then no motion again.
That puts a still point at the top as well as the bottom, which would make the system **fixed at both ends**.
So the next possible mode adds one more piece, for **three** pieces in total, and that ends with motion at the free top again.
The simple version is that the free end must always be moving, and only an odd number of quarter-waves ends on a moving point.

teaching.text: **The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called formants.** A **formant** is a frequency of vibration of a system that is fixed at one end and completely free at the other end. Formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one, and they are written **F1**, **F2** and **F3**.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions

teaching.text: **Counting quarter-wave pieces gives every formant from the first one.** If **F1 is 500 hertz**, then **F2 is three times that, 1500 hertz**, and **F3 is five times that, 2500 hertz**.
children: Each step between formants is twice F1, because each new mode adds two more quarter-wave pieces.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system.** The air in the mouth and throat forms a tube.
children: At one end are the **vocal folds**. The vocal folds are closed, so the air there **cannot move back and forth**. That makes this end **fixed**.
At the other end, the **lips are open**, so the air can move back and forth freely. That makes this end **free**.

teaching.text: **The motion of air in the vocal tract is like the motion of a building**, and the math for both is almost exactly the same.
children: So the frequencies of the air are **formants**, which are odd multiples of the lowest one.
Speaking changes the stiffness and mass of the air in different parts of the tract. That moves the formants, and listeners hear the movement as different vowels and consonants.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: **The air in the tube can be modeled as lines of particles.** Each particle stands for billions of air molecules.
children: Where the lines come **very close together and then very far apart**, the air is compressing and expanding. The air is acting like a **spring**.

Where the lines **move back and forth** without changing their distance from each other, the air is acting like a **mass**. This is easiest to see at the **free end at the lips**, where the air simply moves in and out.
In plain terms, bunching and spreading means springiness, and sliding without bunching means mass.

teaching.text: **The modes of the air match the modes of a building.**
children: In **Mode 1**, the only point of no motion is the fixed end. The air near the fixed end compresses a lot, and the air near the lips moves a lot without compressing. A building in Mode 1 is the same, with lots of compression near the ground and lots of motion near the top.
In **Mode 2**, there are **two points of no motion**, one at the fixed end and one inside the tube.
In **Mode 3**, there are **three points of no motion**. The air around each of those points compresses and expands a lot, so those are the springiest places.

teaching.text: **In Mode 4 of a building, the most springiness is at the four places that do not move.** These are the fixed bottom and the three points where the building's line crosses its resting position. The places between them move the most and have the least springiness.
children: Raising the stiffness at a place that moves the most changes **nothing**, because the structure is not acting like a spring there.
Raising the stiffness at a place that does not move makes the frequency **go up a lot**, because that place is very springy.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction

teaching.text: **Each vowel squeezes the air at a different place.** A **constriction** is a place where the tongue or lips squeeze the air. Locations are measured from the **glottis**, the tiny space between the vocal folds at the fixed end.
children: In **done**, the central vowel, there is **no constriction**, and the air is fairly even along the whole tract.
In **dean**, a **front high vowel**, the air is squeezed under the roof of the mouth, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Don**, a **low back vowel**, the air is squeezed far back, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **dune**, a **back high vowel**, the lips are rounded close together, so the air is squeezed **at the lips**.
**Dan** is a **front low vowel**.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another

teaching.text: **A constriction raises both the stiffness and the mass of the air.**
children: **Squeezing air raises its stiffness**, the same way squeezing a tire makes it stiffer. So a constriction at a place with lots of compression **raises frequency**.
**Squeezing air raises its mass**, because it packs the air into a smaller space and raises its **density**. So a constriction at a place where the air moves a lot **lowers frequency**.

teaching.text: **Even though a constriction raises both, it still changes the formants, because moving places and compressing places take turns.** At any one spot, in any one mode, only the extra mass or only the extra stiffness counts.
children: A reliable way to answer any constriction question is to ask two questions in order. First, is the air at this spot mostly moving or mostly compressing in this mode? Second, which change counts there, the extra mass or the extra stiffness?

teaching.text: **The same two questions answer a question about a string fixed at both ends.** Choose a small spot where **Mode 3 crosses its middle line** while **Mode 4 is at the top of a bump**, and raise both the mass and the stiffness of that spot.
children: In **Mode 3**, the string does not move at that spot but is stretched the most, so only the extra stiffness counts, and **Mode 3's frequency goes up**.
In **Mode 4**, the string moves the most at that spot and hardly stretches, so only the extra mass counts, and **Mode 4's frequency goes down**.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: **Before reasoning about a vowel, it helps to know where the air moves and where it compresses in the first two modes.**
children: In **Mode 1**, the air near the closed glottis end compresses and expands a lot, and the air near the open lip end moves back and forth.
In **Mode 2**, the air compresses a lot at the closed end and again at a second place about two thirds of the way along. In between, about one third of the way along, the air mostly moves.

teaching.text: **The closed end is always springy, and the open end is always massy, in every mode.** Air can be squeezed against a closed end, but there is nothing to squeeze against at an open end.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: **The mass-spring chain marks the three vowel locations along the tube.** **/a/** is one third of the way from the glottis, **/i/** is two thirds of the way, and **/u/** is at the lip end. Each vowel adds mass and stiffness at its own spot, and the effect on F1 and F2 depends on whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.

**Adding mass and stiffness at the very top of a building lowers the frequency of every mode.** The top is the free end, so in every mode the top moves the most and is almost not springy. Only the extra mass counts there.
children: **The top of the building matches the lip end of the vocal tract.** That is why rounding the lips lowers every formant.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: **For /u/, F1 and F2 both go down.** Rounding the lips squeezes the air at the **free end**. The free end moves a lot and hardly compresses in both Mode 1 and Mode 2, so the extra **mass** counts in both modes.
children: A speaker who went from the central vowel into /u/ showed **both formants dropping** in the recording.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **For /i/, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** /i/ squeezes the air about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot has lots of motion, so the extra mass counts and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot has lots of compression, so the extra stiffness counts and **F2 goes up**.
A speaker who went from the central vowel into /i/ showed the **first formant dropping a lot** and the **second formant going up**.
In plain terms, the same squeeze lands on a moving spot for F1 and on a springy spot for F2, so one formant falls while the other rises.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: **For /a/, F1 goes up and F2 goes down, which is the reverse of /i/.** /a/ squeezes the air about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot near the fixed end compresses a lot, so the extra stiffness counts and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot moves a lot, so the extra mass counts and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: **The reasoning also works backward.**
children: If a constriction raises a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be **very springy and hardly moving** in that mode.
If a constriction lowers a formant a lot, the air at that spot must be **moving a lot** in that mode.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: **A schwa matches the prediction for a uniform tube.** A **schwa** is made with no constriction. A measured schwa had formants near **500, 1500 and 2500 hertz**, which are the odd multiples that a uniform fixed-free tube predicts.
children: Every other vowel moves the formants away from these schwa values by changing where the air moves and where the air compresses.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: **Speech uses two vibrating systems at the same time, the source and the filter.**
children: The **vocal folds** are a fixed-fixed system. They are the **source**, and they produce **harmonics**. The lowest harmonic is called the **base frequency**, or **F0**. In this example the harmonics are **100 hertz apart**.
The **air in the vocal tract** is a fixed-free system. It acts as a **filter**, and its frequencies are the **formants**. For the schwa, the formants are near **500, 1500, 2500 and 3500 hertz**.

teaching.text: **The formants decide how tall each harmonic is.** All the harmonics are still there. **Harmonics near a formant are tall, and harmonics far from any formant are short.** The outline of the harmonic heights is called the **envelope**, and the envelope has a peak at each formant.
children: **The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel. Their heights change, and the envelope is what makes each vowel sound different.**
In plain terms, the vocal folds decide which frequencies are present, and the shape of the mouth decides which of those frequencies are loud.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: **The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high, so the two formants are far apart.** In the /i/ spectrum, the tall harmonics are bunched at the very bottom. Next comes a long stretch of short harmonics. The next tall group appears much higher up.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: **The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2, so the two formants are close together.** In the /a/ spectrum, the first two groups of tall harmonics sit close together in the lower part of the spectrum.
children: The same source harmonics are under both /i/ and /a/. Only the filter is different. Moving the constriction moves the formants and changes which harmonics are loud.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: **A spectrogram shows how the spectrum changes over time.** A **spectrum** shows one instant. Speech changes over time, because the tongue and lips keep moving and constrictions are made and released.
children: **Time** runs along the **horizontal axis**.
**Frequency** runs up the **vertical axis**. In a single spectrum, frequency was the horizontal axis.
**Amplitude** is shown as **darkness** on the display. The louder a frequency is, the darker it looks.

teaching.text: **Formants appear as dark bands that move as the speaker moves.** In **/ia/**, the two lowest bands start **far apart** during /i/. As the speaker moves into /a/, **F1 rises and F2 falls**, so the bands **come close together**.
children: Reading a spectrogram means following the dark bands, because the dark bands are the formants changing over time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **"Where were you a year ago?" shows the source and the filter working together over time.** The vocal folds, which are the source, keep producing harmonics. The vocal tract, which is the filter, keeps changing shape. So the envelope over the harmonics changes from moment to moment.
children: On a spectrogram, these changes appear as **dark bands that rise and fall**. The dark bands are the formants, and darkness shows amplitude.
Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, the two lowest bands spread far apart. During "you," all the bands drop because the lips are rounded.

teaching.text: **A spectrum shows one frozen moment, but a spectrogram shows how the formants move.** Real speech is always moving. Reading a sentence means following each band and asking which constriction moved it.

sections.title: Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: **Formants can only be seen through the harmonics, so the spacing of the harmonics matters.** With harmonics every **100 hertz** and formants at **300 and 2100 hertz**, **many harmonics** sit under each formant peak. The formants clearly shape the heights of many harmonics, so the formants are easy to see.

**With a higher base frequency, the formants become hard to see.** With harmonics every **250 hertz**, fewer harmonics land on each formant peak. A formant can even fall **between two harmonics**, so **it becomes very hard to tell the harmonics from the formants**.
children: A **toddler's** harmonics can be at 400, 800 and 1200 hertz. That is why listeners can find a toddler's vowels hard to identify unless they know the child.
A **soprano's** harmonics can start at 800 hertz and continue at 1600 and 2400 hertz, so the words of an opera singer are often very hard to follow.

teaching.text: **Formants are the smooth envelope, and harmonics are samples taken from that envelope.** A higher F0 means fewer samples, so the spectrogram stops looking like clean formant bands.
children: A simple way to see it is that the harmonics are like points used to trace a curve. With many points, the curve is clear. With only a few points, the curve is hard to see.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: **Speech uses two vibrating systems, and the first one is the vocal folds.** The **vocal folds** are a **membrane**, which is a vibrating sheet. The vocal folds are **fixed on all sides** and are made of many masses and springs.
children: The vocal folds vibrate in many modes at once. In Mode 1, all the masses move up and down together. In Mode 2, half move up while the other half move down. Higher modes make more complicated patterns.
All the modes add together into one combined motion. This combined motion is what actually happens in the throat while a person talks.

teaching.text: **Because the vocal folds are fixed-fixed, their frequencies are harmonics.** **Harmonics** are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.
children: The lowest harmonic is called **F0**. Each person has a different F0, but the other harmonics are always multiples of that person's F0.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: **The second vibrating system is the air in the vocal tract, which is fixed at one end and free at the other.**
children: The air is **fixed at the glottis**, because the closed vocal folds keep the air there from moving back and forth.
The air is **free at the lips**, where it can move in and out.
A fixed end and a free end allow only the **odd harmonics**, so the frequencies of the air are one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: **Each fixed-free mode is built from quarter-wave pieces.** Each piece goes from no motion at a still point to the most motion at a moving point.
children: **Mode 1 holds one piece, Mode 2 holds three pieces, Mode 3 holds five pieces, and Mode 4 holds seven pieces.**
Two pieces would end with a still point at the free end, which is impossible. So only odd numbers of pieces fit, and that is why the formants are odd multiples of the first formant.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: **In the vocal tract, the air moves along the tube, not up and down.** This back-and-forth motion along the tube is **longitudinal** motion. Each formant is one mode of this longitudinal motion. F1 is the lowest mode, and F2 is the next mode.
children: The modes look like a building's modes turned on their side. The fixed glottis end is on the left, and the free lip end is on the right.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: **The closed end is always springy, and the open end is always massy, in every mode.** Air can be squeezed against a closed end. Air has nothing to squeeze against at an open end.
children: Near the **closed end**, the thin layers of air come very close together and then far apart. The air **compresses and expands**, so it acts like a **spring**.
Near the **open end**, the thin layers of air stay the same distance apart and just move back and forth. The air acts like a **mass**.
In higher modes, springy places and massy places **take turns** more and more times along the tube.
In plain terms, the lip end swings like a heavy door, and the throat end squeezes like a pillow.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: **Any constriction question can be answered with the same three steps.** Take a spot inside the tube where, in **Mode 3**, the lines of air bunch up and spread apart but hardly move back and forth. Squeezing the tract at that spot raises **F3**.
children: The first step is that squeezing air always **increases both its mass and its stiffness**, the same way squeezing a tire makes it stiffer.
The second step is that, at this spot in Mode 3, the air is acting like a **pure spring**. It compresses and expands but does not move back and forth, so the extra mass does not matter.
The third step is that only the extra stiffness counts, and **raising stiffness raises frequency**, so **F3 goes up**.

teaching.text: **The answer is built one step at a time, not memorized.** Each new spot and each new mode needs the same steps. Each step rests on the step before it, which is how any good argument is built, in science and in art.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: **Images taken during speech show where each vowel squeezes the air.** The vocal tract is a tube from the closed glottis to the open lips.
children: The vowel in **done** has **no constriction** at all.
**dean** squeezes the air near the front, about **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
**Don** squeezes the air far back in the throat, about **one third of the way from the glottis**.
**dune** squeezes the air **at the lips** by rounding them.
**Dan** is a low front vowel.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: **A constriction changes both the inertia of the air and its stiffness.** **Inertia** is the air's resistance to being moved, which is its mass. In the mass-spring model, a constriction is drawn as **heavier masses and stiffer springs** at that spot.
children: A constriction always raises both mass and stiffness. Moving places and springy places take turns, so **the effect depends on what the air is doing at that spot in each mode**.
**When stiffness is what matters at a spot, the frequency goes up. When mass is what matters, the frequency goes down.**

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **The same spot in the tube can act differently in the two modes, so each mode must be checked separately.** A spot can be massy in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2. Then one constriction lowers F1 and raises F2 at the same time.
children: That is why a vowel is identified by the pair of formants, not by one formant alone.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: **For /u/, F1 and F2 both go down.** /u/ squeezes the air at the lips. At the open end, the air moves back and forth with almost no compression in **every** mode, so the air there acts as a pure mass. The extra stiffness does not matter, and the extra mass does.
children: The schwa has reference values of about **500 and 1500 hertz**. A measured /u/ had an F1 in the low two hundreds, well below 500.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: **For /i/, F1 goes down and F2 goes up.** /i/ squeezes the air about two thirds of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air at that spot moves back and forth, so it acts like a mass. The extra mass counts, and **F1 goes down**.
In **Mode 2**, the air at that spot compresses and expands, so it acts like a spring. The extra stiffness counts, and **F2 goes up**.
A speaker going from schwa into /i/ showed exactly this, with **F1 going down and F2 going up**.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: **For /a/, F1 goes up and F2 goes down.** /a/ squeezes the air about one third of the way from the glottis.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot is close enough to the closed end that the air is mostly springy. The extra stiffness counts, and **F1 goes up**.
In **Mode 2**, that spot sits between two springy regions, so the air there mostly moves. The extra mass counts, and **F2 goes down**.
A speaker producing /a/ showed **F1 going up and F2 going down**. In a typical /a/, F1 and F2 are fairly close together.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: **All three vowels follow one rule. Find whether the air at the constriction mostly moves or mostly compresses in each mode, then decide whether the extra mass or the extra stiffness counts.**
children: At the lips, the air is massy in both modes, so /u/ lowers both formants.
Two thirds along the tube, the air is massy in Mode 1 and springy in Mode 2, so /i/ lowers F1 and raises F2.
One third along the tube, the air is springy in Mode 1 and massy in Mode 2, so /a/ raises F1 and lowers F2.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are the source, and their mass and stiffness set F0 and the spacing of the harmonics.**
children: **Big, heavy, loose vocal folds** have a large mass and a small stiffness, so their **F0 is low**, around 100 hertz, with harmonics at 200, 300 and so on.
**Tighter, lighter vocal folds** have a higher F0, such as 250 hertz, with harmonics at 500 and 750 hertz.
**Very tight, light vocal folds** have an even higher F0, such as 350 hertz, with harmonics at 700 and 1050 hertz.

teaching.text: **F0 keeps changing while people talk.** Only a robot keeps F0 constant. Speakers change F0 by tightening and loosening the vocal folds with the muscles in the larynx, and listeners use those changes to understand meaning.
children: When **"The dog slept here"** is a statement, F0 falls at the very end. When the same words are a question, F0 rises at the end.
The way F0 moves also tells listeners whether a person is being sarcastic, pretending, or even lying.

teaching.text: **F0 can be measured in Praat.** Take a short piece of speech, view a spectral slice, and pick the lowest harmonic. One measured voice had F0 around 170 hertz, and the next harmonic was at about twice that value, as the theory predicts.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: **The air in the vocal tract is the filter, and the formants depend on where the constriction is.** Typical values show the patterns.
children: **Schwa** has F1 near **500** and F2 near **1500** hertz.
**/u/** has F1 near 300, F2 near 1000 and F3 near 2000 hertz, so all of them are lower.
**/i/** has F1 near 300 and F2 near 2200 hertz, so they are very far apart.
**/a/** has F1 and F2 both near 800 to 900 hertz, so they are very close together.

teaching.text: **The main rule is that a formant makes the nearby harmonics loud, and harmonics far from any formant are muted.** During a schwa, harmonics near 500 hertz are loud. The farther a harmonic is from 500, the weaker it is. Between two formants the harmonics get weaker, and near the next formant they get stronger again.
children: **The vowel shape is the filter. The voice supplies the harmonics, and the filter chooses which harmonics survive.**

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: **The lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants can shape.** Heavy, loose vocal folds give harmonics every 100 hertz. Many harmonics sit under each formant, so the shaped spectrum follows the formant peaks smoothly and is easy to read.

**With very light, tight vocal folds, the harmonics are far apart, so a formant can be missed.** A formant at 500 hertz may have **no harmonic near it to make loud**. Sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it unclear.
children: An **opera singer** is an extreme case. The harmonics are so far apart that the formants do not line up with any harmonic, so listeners struggle to hear which vowel is being sung. Singers are even trained to shape the mouth so the formants line up with the harmonics.

A **small child** of two or three has an F0 near 500 hertz, so very few harmonics fall near the formants. A child's speech is very hard to understand unless the listener is a caretaker who is used to it.
A simple way to see it is that the formants are the same in every case, but a high voice gives the listener only a few harmonics to hear them through.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: **A spectrogram shows how speech changes over time.** **Time** runs along the horizontal axis. **Frequency** runs up the vertical axis. **Darkness** shows how much energy, or amplitude, there is.
children: Each moment of the spectrogram is one spectrum turned on its side, and the spectra are lined up one after another in time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: **"Where were you a year ago?" brings every idea about speech together in one short sentence.** The vocal folds supply harmonics the whole time. Every new sound changes where the tongue and lips squeeze the air, so the formants keep moving from one moment to the next.
children: On a spectrogram of the sentence, **time** runs along the bottom, **frequency** runs up, and the **dark bands are the formants**.
Where the vowel sounds like **/i/**, **F2 rises high and F1 stays low**, because the squeeze is at a spot that is springy in Mode 2 and massy in Mode 1.
During "you," the formants **drop**, because rounding the lips adds mass right where the air moves the most, and that lowers all of them.
Through "a year ago," F2 goes up and then down again as the tongue moves from one vowel to the next.

teaching.text: **All the formants keep changing during speech, so speech is not a string of frozen vowels.** Every rise and fall of a formant can be predicted with the same mass-spring steps. Find the constriction, then check whether the air there is moving or compressing in each mode.
children: This constant change is why a network that sees two formants from one frozen moment cannot understand real speech. Speech recognition needs systems that take in whole stretches of sound over time.
In plain terms, a spectrogram of a real sentence is a moving record of the tongue and lips, and reading it means following the dark bands as they rise and fall.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: **Listeners identify a consonant from the vowel that comes after it, as a spliced recording proves.** A speaker said **ma** and **na**. The **m** part of "ma" was cut out and joined to the **a** part of "na." The consonant came from "ma," so the result should sound like "ma," but **listeners clearly hear "na."**
**The m or n is heard more from the vowel than from the nasal sound itself.** The vowel's formants are different depending on the consonant before the vowel.
children: After **m**, one formant of the vowel stays fairly **steady**.
After **n**, that formant **drops sharply** at the start of the vowel.
So the vowel carries the information about the consonant. Listeners decide which consonant they heard **during the vowel**, after the consonant is already over.

teaching.text: **Listeners take in whole stretches of speech and decide about the sounds that came first using the sounds that follow.** This was one of the first striking results in speech perception, published in the **1950s** by the linguist **André Malécot**.
children: For about seventy years, speech recognition machines treated each slice of sound by itself, and they **failed**, despite billions of dollars of effort.

A machine that understands speech has to use the sound that follows to decide about the sound that came before. That is why modern speech recognition uses large language models built from many neural networks.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: **A neural network can learn to recognize vowels from formants.** The network has **two inputs**, **F1 and F2**, measured from real recordings of five vowels. The network's job is to decide which vowel was spoken.
children: **The network's knowledge is stored in its weights.** The weights are learned from the data.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: **The vowel network has five outputs and three hidden layers.** There is one output neuron for each word, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**. The **three hidden layers** have **3, 2 and 4 neurons**.
children: Information enters at the input, a little like sound reaching the ear.
Each hidden layer turns the numbers it receives into new numbers, a little like the stages of processing in the brain.
The output layer gives the network's decision about which vowel it heard.

teaching.text: **Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is fully connected.** This version is **purely linear**, which means it has **no activation functions**. Each neuron just passes on the result of its inner product.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: **Before training, every weight is a random number between minus one and one.** A **positive** weight makes its input push the next neuron up. A **negative** weight makes its input push the next neuron down.
**The example input is F1 of 320 hertz and F2 of 2000 hertz.** A very low F1 with a very high F2 is the pattern of **/i/**, so the correct answer is **dean**.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: **Forward propagation carries the input through the network one layer at a time.** Each neuron computes an **inner product**, which means multiplying each incoming number by its weight and adding the results.
children: For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, F1 is multiplied by its weight, F2 is multiplied by its weight, and the two results are added.
The first hidden layer produces three numbers. Those three numbers go through the next weights to make two numbers, then four, then five at the output.
The calculations never need to be done by hand. What matters is that every step is an inner product.

teaching.text: **The output is a probability distribution, and with random weights the network is wrong.** The five outputs are **.5, .1, .1, .1 and .2**, which add up to one. The highest probability is on **done**, but the correct answer is dean.
children: The correct answer is given as the target **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**, which puts all the probability on dean.
**Stochastic gradient descent** changes each weight, so that the next time the network sees 320 and 2000, the inner products give a high probability for dean.
In plain terms, the network starts by guessing, the target shows the right answer, and learning nudges every weight so the right answer wins next time.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: **PyTorch describes the network as a list of layers.** **Sequential** means the network has **one layer after another**. **Linear** means the layer **does inner products** of weights and the previous activations.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** means **take input from 2 neurons and have 3 neurons**. The next lines read 3 in and 2 out, then 2 in and 4 out, then 4 in and 5 out.
Setting the **bias** to False keeps every layer purely linear, which matches the diagram of the network. This code only describes the network. It does not train it.

teaching.text: **Only layers that do calculations get a line of code.** The **input layer** has no weights coming into it and does no inner products. The input layer only receives numbers, so it never gets its own line. The first line describes the **first hidden layer**.
children: This network has **five layers in total**, which are the input layer, three hidden layers and the output layer.
This network has **three hidden layers**, and the **last line is always the output layer**.
"How many layers" and "how many hidden layers" are different questions, so read each question carefully.

teaching.text: **To add a hidden layer of 3 neurons right before the output, change only the end.** The first three lines stay the same. The old last line, 4 in and 5 out, becomes **4 in and 3 out**. A new last line takes **3 in and gives 5 out**.
children: A quick check is that each line's first number must match the previous line's second number, because each layer takes its input from the layer before it.

teaching.text: **The same reading works for any network written this way.** A network written as 4 in and 3 out, 3 in and 8 out, 8 in and 4 out, 4 in and 4 out, and 4 in and 5 out takes **4 numbers as input**, has **four hidden layers** with 3, 8, 4 and 4 neurons, and chooses among **5 categories**.
children: Drawn as a network, it has a column of **4 input neurons**, then hidden columns of **3, 8, 4 and 4 neurons**, then a column of **5 output neurons**.
When the first category is correct, the target puts a **1 in the first slot and 0 in every other slot**.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: **A neural network can work as a simple speech recognizer that decides which vowel it heard.** The network takes the **two formants**, **F1 and F2**, of a vowel. It decides which of **five words** it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**.
children: Networks like this one were the kind used fifteen or twenty years ago.
Modern **large language models** are built from many networks like this one, the way molecules are built from **atoms**.

teaching.text: **The network has an input layer, three hidden layers and an output layer.** There are **2 input neurons**, **hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons**, and **5 output neurons**. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is **fully connected**.
children: The **input neurons** only take in numbers. One speaker's F1 might be 400 and F2 might be 1900 for some vowel.
**The network's knowledge is stored in its weights.** Each connection has a weight, which is a positive or negative number. The whole network is a machine that processes numbers using those weights.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation carries one input through the network to a decision.** The example input is **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, which is the pattern of **dean**.
children: Each neuron computes an **inner product**. For the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the weight on F1 is multiplied by 320, the weight on F2 is multiplied by 2000, and the two results are added.
The result of that inner product, with nothing else done to it, is called the neuron's **linear activation**. Here it comes out slightly below zero.
Each layer's activations become the inputs to the next layer. The next layer does more inner products, and this continues until the output layer.

teaching.text: **At the end, the output numbers are turned into a probability distribution, which is the network's decision.** A **probability distribution** is a set of numbers between zero and one that **add up to one**. The step that makes this distribution is called **softmax**.
children: The only thing to know about softmax is that a bigger number gives a bigger probability.
Probabilities and percentages are the same idea. A probability of 0.55 is a 55 percent chance.
Here the network gives **done about 56 percent** and much less to the other words. So the network decides it heard done, even though the input was dean.

teaching.text: **The network's knowledge is just positive and negative numbers, and its decisions come from multiplying and adding.** Multiplying and adding are second-grade operations. **Inference** means working out a decision, and the AI systems people use every day make decisions with these simple operations.
children: Brains are chemical machines, so this is less surprising than it sounds. The chemistry of ions such as sodium, potassium and calcium inside neurons does operations close to adding and multiplying.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: **The effect of raising one number can be worked out without doing any arithmetic, because every step is an inner product.** Take the top neuron of the last hidden layer. Its activation is about 1.57, and its weight into the **done** output is positive 0.1.
children: If that **activation goes up**, the activation times the positive weight goes up, so the **probability of done goes up**.
If that **weight goes up**, from 0.1 to 0.2, the same product grows, so the **probability of done goes up** again.
The rule is that **a positive number times a positive number is positive**. So raising either one makes that neuron push the done output up more.

teaching.text: **A good exam answer names the direction first and then gives the reason.** For example, the probability of done goes up because the weight and the activation are both positive, so their product adds more to the done output. The exam never asks for the multiplication itself.
children: In plain terms, each neuron votes for each output through its weight, and a positive vote from an active neuron always helps that output.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Every network starts out knowing nothing, because its weights start out random.** The network only improves when it is told the right answer.
children: The right answer is given as a **desired output**. For a recording of dean, the desired output is **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**. That says there is a 100 percent chance it was dean and zero for every other word. A list with a single one and zeros everywhere else is called a **one-hot encoding**.
The output the network actually produced is the **computed output**. The difference between the computed output and the desired output is the network's **error**.
The desired outputs come from real data, such as a table of each student's formants and the vowel that student actually said.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation is the method that changes the weights so the network makes better decisions.** After learning, if 320 and 2000 are given again, the probability of done should go down and the probability of dean should go up.
children: **Learning happens gradually, one small step at a time.** As in stochastic gradient descent, the weights do not jump to the right values at once. Each piece of data nudges the weights a little.
Each weight moves a small step in whichever direction makes the error smaller. The **learning rate** sets the size of each step.

The weights are updated **starting from the end**. First the weights into the output change, then the weights into the third hidden layer, then the second, then the first. The activations from the forward pass stay the same during this backward pass.

teaching.text: **This is why AI needs huge data centers.** A modern chatbot can have **trillions of weights**. Backpropagation has to nudge every one of them, over and over, for months.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: **For the last weight, it is easy to tell which way to change it.** The last weight is the 0.1 that connects the top neuron of the last hidden layer to **done**.
children: That weight multiplies an activation of about 1.57, so raising the weight would raise the probability of done.
The desired probability of done is **zero**, so raising the weight would make the error **worse**.
So that weight should be **lowered**, which pulls the probability of done toward zero. Only one inner product is needed to work this out.

teaching.text: **For the first weight, it is very hard to tell which way to change it.** The first weight is the 0.005 near the input.
children: Changing it changes one activation in the first hidden layer. That changes the second hidden layer, which changes the third, which finally changes the output probabilities.

**Its effect on the decision passes through every layer in between**, and it also depends on all the later weights. So looking at the first weight alone cannot show whether it should go up or down. Backpropagation still works it out.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Backpropagation starts at the end because the last weights are the easiest problem.**
children: **The last weights decide the output probabilities directly**, so the error can be used right away to improve them.

**The first weights affect their activations, which affect two more layers of activations.** It is very hard to tell how much an early weight is to blame for a mistake at the end. The effect of an early weight also **includes the effect of the last weights**, which come after it.

teaching.text: **Improving the last weights is the easy problem, and improving the first weights is a bigger problem that contains the easy one.** The method for solving small problems first and then reusing their answers for bigger problems is **dynamic programming**, developed by **Bellman** and **Viterbi**.
children: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.** Stochastic gradient descent changes the numbers gradually. Dynamic programming supplies the order, which is the "back" in backpropagation.
Backpropagation was worked out in the **mid-1980s**. In 2024 a Nobel Prize recognized it, because there would be no AI without it.
Research from the last ten years suggests that single neurons in the brain also work forward and then backward, using their chemistry.

teaching.text: **The short exam answer is this.** The last weight affects the decision in one simple step. The first weight's effect passes through many layers and depends on the later weights. So the easy problem is solved first, and its answer is reused for the harder problems.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: **Training needs two tables of numbers, called matrices, and each row pairs one recording with its true vowel.**
children: The **input matrix** has one row per recording and **two columns**, F1 and F2, because the network takes two numbers in. With about 110 recordings, the input matrix is 110 by 2.
The **output matrix** has one row per recording and **five columns**, one for each word. A **1 marks the true vowel**, and the other columns hold 0. The output matrix is 110 by 5.
So each row tells the network the right answer. Formants like 800 and 1700 go with one vowel, and formants like 700 and 1100 go with another.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: **A short Python program using the PyTorch library builds the network and runs one training step.**
children: The **import** lines tell the program to use the **torch library**. The library does all the background work, so the network can be described in a few lines.
The two **load** lines read the two matrices from files. The formants become X, and the true vowels become Y.

teaching.text: **The layer lines describe the network.** **Sequential** means the network is a **sequence of layers**, one after another. **Linear** means the layer **does inner products**, because a linear layer only multiplies and adds.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)** describes the **first hidden layer**, which takes **2 inputs and gives 3 outputs**. The next lines take 3 and give 2, take 2 and give 4, and take 4 and give 5.

The network has **five layers** but only **four lines**, because the **input layer does no processing**. The input layer only receives numbers, so its only trace in the code is the 2 in the first line.

teaching.text: **The last lines run one training step using all 110 rows at once.**
children: **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent. **lr** is the **learning rate**, which sets the size of each step.
The **loss** measures the network's mistakes by comparing its outputs with the true vowels.
**backward** runs backpropagation to work out how each weight should change, and **step** actually changes the weights.
In plain terms, the program describes the network, shows it the data, measures how wrong it is, works backward to find which weights caused the mistake, and then adjusts the weights a little.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Real neurons are nearly digital, either on or off, and the sigmoid copies that.** **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932** for discovering that **neurons are nearly digital**. A real neuron is roughly **on or off**, firing or not firing. The neurons in the network so far are not like that, because their activations can be any number, such as slightly below zero, about 6.6, or about 2.7.
**The sigmoid is an activation function that squashes an inner product into a number between zero and one.**
children: A **large negative** inner product gives about **0**, so the neuron is **off**. Minus 4, minus 10, minus 100 and minus 1000 all give about zero.
A **large positive** inner product gives about **1**, so the neuron is **on**. 4, 6 and 100 all give about one.
Only inner products **near zero** give values in between. So the sigmoid **makes the neuron nearly digital**, like the chemistry that keeps real neurons from firing without limit.

teaching.text: **The sigmoid also matches how perception works.** **Some things that are very different are perceived as the same, and some things that are very similar are perceived as different.**
children: A friend is recognized as the same person with a hat or without one, or in a different shirt on a different day. Perception ignores real differences, the same way the sigmoid gives minus 1000, minus 100 and minus 20 the same value.

USC and UCLA are both large universities with similar labs and football, yet people perceive them as completely different. A small difference can matter a lot, the same way two inputs just below and just above zero land on opposite sides of the sigmoid's jump.
In plain terms, the flat parts of the curve treat different things as the same, and the steep middle separates nearly identical things.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: **Adding the sigmoid to each hidden neuron changes every number after it.** The inputs stay as formants, but each hidden neuron now passes on its sigmoid value instead of its raw inner product.
children: The first hidden neuron's inner product, slightly below zero, becomes about **0.4**.
The second, about 6.6, becomes about **1**, so that neuron is fully on.
Each time a neuron changes, the activations in the later layers are recalculated, and the output probabilities shift.

teaching.text: **With the same random weights and the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons, the network is still wrong.** The network spreads its probability more evenly and gives its highest probability, about one third, to **Dan**. The sigmoid changes how the network calculates, but only training with backpropagation can give it good weights.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: **The program changes in only one way. nn.Sigmoid is added after each hidden linear layer.** nn.Sigmoid means "apply the sigmoid," which makes that layer nearly digital.
children: The **last layer has no sigmoid**, because its outputs go straight into the loss calculation, which turns them into probabilities.
The rest of the training program, with SGD and a learning rate of 0.1, stays the same.

teaching.text: **Training both versions tests whether the sigmoid makes the vowel recognizer better or worse.** Other activation functions that look somewhat like the sigmoid, such as **ReLU**, can be swapped in to test them too.
children: **Many of the most basic ideas in AI come from how real brains work.** Neurons, inner products that gather input from many neurons, and nearly digital firing all come from the brain.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: **This network copies a simple piece of human perception, deciding which vowel it heard.** The network takes the **two formants**, F1 and F2, of a single vowel. It decides which of five words it heard, **done, dune, dean, Don or Dan**.
children: The network has 2 input neurons, hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and 5 output neurons. Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

teaching.text: **The weights are the network's knowledge, and the network learns by correcting mistakes.** Each weight is a positive or negative number. The network is told the right answer for each recording as a probability distribution. For a speaker's /i/, the right answer is **0, 0, 1, 0, 0**, which means a 100 percent chance that the word was dean.
children: At first **the weights are random**, so the network knows nothing, and its output is usually very different from the right answer.
The difference between the output and the right answer is a **mistake**. The network learns by correcting its mistakes.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation carries the input through the network, one layer at a time.** Take **F1 of 320 and F2 of 2000**, which is one speaker's /i/.
children: Each neuron in the first hidden layer computes an **inner product**. It multiplies each formant by its weight and adds the results.
Those activations go into the next layer, which does its own inner products. This continues until the output gives one probability for each word.

teaching.text: **With random weights, the network is wrong.** The network gives more than half of its probability to **done**, so it decides it heard done. The right answer is dean.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: **The last weights are the easiest to change, because they connect directly to the decision.** The output probabilities are the network's decision, and the last weights are the weights used in the final inner products.
children: For example, the probability of done comes partly from a weight of 0.1 times an activation of about 1.57.
The network said done, but the answer was dean, so the probability of done is **too high**.
Raising that 0.1 to 0.5 would raise the probability of done, which is the opposite of what is wanted. So that weight should go **down**.

teaching.text: **The first weights are the hardest to change, because their effect passes through every layer.** Changing a weight near the input changes the first hidden layer, which changes the second, which changes the third, which finally changes the decision.

sections.title: Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: **The real formant data from the class shows why AI is hard.** Each recording is a dot. **F1** is on the horizontal axis, and **F2** is on the vertical axis. There are 525 dots, 105 for each vowel.
children: The data has a pattern. The **/i/ dots sit high**, with a **high F2 and a low F1**, as the theory predicts. /i/ is clearly different from /u/.
The data also has **a lot of overlap**. Many /æ/ dots sit among the /i/ dots, and many others overlap with schwa. The /u/, /a/ and schwa groups pile on top of each other.
Some dots are probably measurement mistakes. Real data always has errors, the same way speech to a phone on a noisy train has errors, so the dots were left in.

teaching.text: **If each vowel formed its own separate group, AI would be easy.** Because the groups overlap, a network has to see the data many times to learn where each vowel is most likely. Even then, many points are unclear.
children: For a new speaker whose formants land in the middle of the overlap, the best answer is the vowel whose dots are most common there.

Removing the differences between speakers is called **normalization**. People tried it for about seventy years without success. Hearing a lot of speech from the same speaker does help, because it gives the system more information about that person.

teaching.text: **This overlap was first discovered in the early 1950s by Peterson and Barney.** Spectrograms had been kept secret by the military during the Second World War, and the overlap was found once spectrograms became available.
children: Good speech recognition only arrived around 2011 or 2012, using neural networks trained by backpropagation.
Surprisingly, speech that changes over time turned out to be easier for modern systems than this frozen, one-moment problem. Large language models use information from before and after each moment.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation changes all the weights using two tools, stochastic gradient descent and dynamic programming.**
children: **Stochastic gradient descent** is the same method used to improve an average from data. Here it improves every weight. It has the same **learning rate**, with the same tradeoff between learning fast and learning accurately.

**Dynamic programming** decides the order. The weights at the end are improved first, then the weights before them, and so on back to the beginning. The easiest problem is solved first and the hardest problem is solved last.

teaching.text: **The error says which way each output should move.** Done, at about 56 percent, should go down, dean should go up, and the other words should go down.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: **For the last weights, one inner product is enough to decide the direction.** The network said done when the answer was dean. So any last weight that pushes done up should be **lowered**, and any last weight that pushes dean up should be raised.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Backpropagation changes the last weights first, then the weights before them, back to the first weights.** Each problem is easier because something was already learned from the problems solved before it.
children: Modern systems apply this to about **six trillion weights**, which is what huge data centers are doing.
**Geoffrey Hinton** won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for backpropagation. The idea is at the center of much of today's economy, and it has roots in physics through dynamical systems.
In plain terms, blame for a mistake is easiest to assign to the weights closest to the mistake. That blame is then passed backward to the weights that came before.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: **Training uses two matrices of numbers, one for the formants and one for the true vowels.** The first matrix has one row per recording with **F1 and F2**. The second matrix has the matching row of **zeros and a single one** that marks the true vowel.
children: Learning picks a row, computes the network's decision, and compares it with the true answer.
If the decision is wrong, the weights change.

teaching.text: **If the network makes the right decision, there is no error, so there is nothing to learn.** This can be a real problem. A network can keep getting the right answer by **memorizing** its data without learning the pattern underneath. Stopping the learning at that point would be stopping too early.
**Children learning English show the same pattern, as Carol Chomsky observed in the early 1960s.**
children: First, very young children say **go** and **went** correctly, because they are **memorizing** what they hear.
Second, they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs form the past by adding a sound at the end, as in **jump** and **jumped**. So they start saying **goed**.
Third, they learn that some verbs are **exceptions**, and they get both the regular verbs and the exceptions right.
In plain terms, a right answer early on can come from memory, and real learning can show up as new mistakes.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: **The program's lines each have a job, and the exam can ask what the lines mean, but never how to write the program from scratch.**
children: **The import lines bring into Python the programs for inner products, backpropagation and related work**, so none of it has to be written by hand.

This works because of **libraries**, which are collections of programs written by one group that other people can use without knowing how they work inside. The idea of software built from parts like this goes back to **Margaret Hamilton's** software for **Apollo 11**.

Around 2015, **Facebook** released **PyTorch** and **Google** released **TensorFlow**, so researchers no longer had to write their own backpropagation code. Most people now use PyTorch, often called torch.
The **load** lines read the formant matrix and the vowel matrix from files.
