teaching.text: **Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers, one after another.** Every network covered so far is a sequence of layers. A large language model is an example of a network that is not just a sequence of layers.
children: Each **Linear** line is one **processing layer**. A processing layer has weights and does inner products with the incoming numbers.
The input layer does no processing, so the five layers need only **four lines**.
**nn.Linear(2, 3)** means "receive information from 2 neurons, and have 3 neurons." The other lines read the same way.

teaching.text: **The last lines are all PyTorch needs for learning.**
children: **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent. **lr** is the **learning rate**, set here to 0.1.

**A higher learning rate learns much faster but less accurately. A lower learning rate learns more accurately but much more slowly.** So changing the learning rate from 0.1 to 0.3 makes the network learn faster, but its accuracy goes down.
**Loss** is the measure of the **mistake**. The program calculates the mistakes so it can learn from them.
**backward** runs **backpropagation**, and **step** updates the weights.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **The sigmoid makes neurons nearly digital, like real neurons.** Artificial networks borrow their basic ideas from real brains. Real brains have **neurons**, and each neuron **gathers information from many other neurons**, which is what the inner product does.

**Lord Edgar Adrian discovered in the 1920s that neurons are nearly digital, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1932.** A real neuron is either **firing** or **not firing**, not at some in-between level like 2, 16 or 34. The network's neurons so far are not like that, because their activations are numbers like slightly below zero, 6.64, 2.72 and 1.57.
**The sigmoid takes an inner product and gives back a number between zero and one.**
children: An inner product of **minus 4**, minus 6 or minus 1000 gives about **zero**, so the neuron is **off**.
An inner product of **2** gives about 0.8 or 0.9. An inner product of **4**, 6 or 100 gives about **one**, so the neuron is **on**.
So the sigmoid makes neural processing nearly digital, the way brain chemistry does. Without that limit, an activation of a thousand would be like lightning coming out of someone's head.

teaching.text: **The sigmoid also matches perception.** **Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.** Very different large negative inputs all come out as off. Two nearly equal inputs on either side of the steep middle come out as off and on.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: **Adding the sigmoid one hidden neuron at a time changes the whole calculation after it.** Each neuron's raw inner product is replaced by its sigmoid value. Every later activation is recalculated, and the output probabilities shift.
children: The first hidden neuron, slightly below zero, becomes about 0.4. The second, about 6.6, becomes nearly 1.
With the sigmoid on all nine hidden neurons and the same random weights, the network's choice moves from done to Dan. The network is still wrong until it is trained.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: **In the program, nn.Sigmoid is added after each hidden linear layer.** nn.Sigmoid means "apply the sigmoid," which makes that layer nearly digital. The last layer gets no sigmoid, because its outputs go into the loss calculation.
children: The sigmoid can be replaced by other functions that look somewhat like it, such as **ReLU**, to test whether recognition gets better or worse.
**AI copies abilities that animals have.** Its most basic ideas come from biologists' discoveries about how brains work. Computer scientists then add their own ideas on top.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: **The full training program runs 2000 updates and records the accuracy after each one.** Each update uses all the recordings, with a learning rate of 0.1. The formants are divided by a thousand first, which turns hertz into kilohertz.
children: **Accuracy** is the percent of recordings the network classifies correctly. The word with the largest score counts as the network's answer.

teaching.text: **The accuracy starts at 20 percent, which is chance.** With random weights, the network knows nothing. With **five vowels**, a random guess is right **one time out of five**, which is 20 percent. This level is called **chance**.
children: With **ten categories**, chance would be **10 percent**, because a random guess would be right one time in ten.

teaching.text: **After a while, the accuracy jumps up to about 40 percent and then levels off near 45 percent.** The jump shows the network is learning something. Each pass of learning is called an **epoch**, and a problem like this takes thousands of epochs.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: **Ten training runs from ten different starting points all end at the same accuracy.** Each run started from a **different set of random weights**. A starting set of random numbers is called a **seed**, though the word itself will not be asked.
children: The runs take **different paths**. One run stays at chance for about 500 epochs before jumping up. Another run jumps up very early. Another run climbs more slowly.
**All ten runs end at the same accuracy**, close to 45 percent. Stochastic gradient descent always involves chance along the way, but the end point is the same.

teaching.text: **Children learning language are similar.** One child's home might talk mostly about sports, and another child's home might talk mostly about politics. Each child hears very different words and voices. By about age four, both children speak the same language, because the basic patterns underneath their different inputs are the same.

**The network levels off near 40 percent, not 100 percent, because the vowel data overlap so much.** For a point in the middle of the overlap, even a person looking carefully would have to guess. AI is not magic, so a problem that is very hard for people is also hard for machines.
children: The next experiment is to add or remove layers, or change the number of neurons in each layer, to see whether the 40 percent gets better or worse.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: **Early neural networks could only make one decision from one fixed list of numbers.** A **neural network** takes in information about one moment, uses its **weights** to process that information, and makes a decision. It learns its weights by making mistakes and correcting them with **backpropagation**.
**The idea began in 1943 with a paper by McCulloch and Pitts.** The paper proposed that simple math could model how the brain works.
children: The paper starts from the **all-or-none** behavior of neurons. All means active, and none means inactive, so a neuron is either firing or not firing.
All-or-none is the same idea as the **sigmoid**. So the very first paper on artificial neural networks started from biology, from how real neurons behave.
Warren McCulloch was a **psychiatrist**. The earliest work on neural networks tried to model how the mind works, including mental illness, and was not about making money.

teaching.text: **By 1986, the ideas had grown into the two Parallel Distributed Processing books, written by a group at UC San Diego.**
children: **Parallel** means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time.
**Distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons.
By 1986, forward propagation and backpropagation were well worked out. One contributor, **Geoffrey Hinton**, later won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for this work.

teaching.text: **The limit of these networks is that they take one fixed list of numbers, but human thinking unfolds over time.** A **vector** is a list of numbers. A **static** vector is one fixed list from one moment. A network like this can take a static vector of formants and choose among a few categories.
children: **Speech changes all the time**, because every small moment has new formants.
**Language also changes over time**, because a sentence is many words, one after another.
So one list of numbers can never model thinking that unfolds over time.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production

teaching.text: **Michael Jordan invented the recurrent neural network in 1985 to model how speech is produced over time.** **Speech production** means how the tongue, the velum and the lips move during speech. Features such as nasality, backness and lip rounding switch on and off at different moments across a sequence of sounds. Jordan saw that a regular network could not handle something that complex and that changes so much over time.
children: Jordan's network is **not only sequential**. It has **two layers working side by side**.

It is called **recurrent** because it **sends its own output back into part of its input**. It produces something at one moment, then uses that output to predict the next moment, and then the moment after that.

teaching.text: **GPT works the same way, one word at a time.**
children: First, GPT takes the words of the prompt and predicts the next word. That word becomes the first word of its answer.
Second, GPT feeds the prompt plus that new word back in and predicts the next word again.
Third, GPT keeps repeating this. So the idea behind GPT began in 1985 with thinking about how speech unfolds over time.
People kept improving the recurrent network from 1985 until **2017**, when the **large language model** was invented.

teaching.text: **Science and technology grow from other people's ideas over long periods of time.** An idea from 1943 was improved into the networks of 1986. Jordan's idea from 1985 was improved into the large language models of 2017. The people who came up with these ideas were mostly not the people who made a lot of money from them.
children: These years give a sense of the history, but they will not be asked about on the exam.

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems

teaching.text: **AI systems are built in levels, and each level is made of the level below it.**
children: **A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results, which is the **inner product**. The symbol **sigma** means add them up. This simple multiplying and adding models the electrochemical activity of a real neuron.

**A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a whole vector of decisions.** Its layers are connected by sets of weights. Each set of weights turns one vector into the next vector through many inner products.

teaching.text: **A large language model takes in many vectors, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision about what comes next.** Picture 15 vectors, each one standing for one word of a sentence. The job of the model is to **predict the sixteenth**.
children: In real systems, there are hundreds of thousands to a million input vectors, and this set is called the **context window**. Each vector is also thousands of numbers long, which is why huge data centers are needed.
The sixteenth vector is a **probability distribution over the next word**. English has about 30,000 words, and each entry gives the chance that one particular word comes next.

teaching.text: **A large language model is made of neural networks, and its knowledge is still in its weights.** Each set of weights is a **layer**, and real systems have about a hundred or more layers. An LLM's knowledge of how to write an essay is stored in its weights.
**An LLM is a dynamical system, which is why the Nobel Prize for AI was given in physics.**
children: A mass-spring system starts from **initial conditions**, and the rule decides what happens next.
An LLM's initial condition is its set of input vectors. Each layer turns those vectors into **better vectors**, step after step, until the last layer can predict the next word.
The calculation at every step is the **inner product**, repeated billions or trillions of times.
In plain terms, an LLM is like the oscillator, except that thousands of numbers are improved layer by layer instead of two numbers changing over time.

teaching.text: **An LLM learns by predicting the next word and correcting its mistakes.**
children: Take "the cat sat on the," where the real next word is **mat**. A new LLM with random weights might predict an impossible word like "in."
Backpropagation adjusts the trillions of weights so the prediction moves toward mat.

After this is repeated with about a trillion sentences, the system can speak English. No philosopher or cognitive scientist expected that human language could be copied using only inner products and functions like the sigmoid.
The first problem this design solved, in 2017, was **machine translation**. The same design then worked for speech and many other problems.

teaching.text: **An agentic system is a group of LLMs connected to each other, and an agent in AI today is just an LLM.**
children: An **outline LLM** receives the prompt and only makes an outline of the answer.
A **writing LLM** turns the outline into full sentences.
A **critic LLM** checks the draft for problems. A **revision LLM** decides whether the draft is good enough or sends it back to the critic. This back-and-forth is usually limited to a few rounds.
A **final LLM** produces the answer the user sees.
The critic greatly reduced **hallucination**, which is when the system makes things up. The conversation between the LLMs is why many systems take a while to respond.

teaching.text: **The levels of AI match the levels of living things.** **Neurons make neural networks, neural networks make LLMs, and LLMs make agentic systems**, the same way molecules make cells and cells make organs.
children: Designing a group of LLMs to solve a problem is a real job today. The job needs problem solving more than knowledge of programming languages.

The connections between LLMs can also form paths that nobody planned. These paths let a system call other LLMs and do things that were not part of the design, sometimes harmful things. Limiting those connections needs creative people from many fields.

teaching.text: **The main idea behind all of this is Gestalt completion.** People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though no triangle is drawn, because a large part of human knowledge is **completing** what is missing. Training a system only to **predict the missing piece** turns out to copy human thinking.
children: The same idea is behind the **cloze procedure**, a test introduced by **Wilson Taylor** in **1953**. In a cloze test, words are removed from a text and people fill them in. The name comes from **closure**, the Gestalt word for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a broken circle as whole.
**Knowledge can be tested by asking someone to complete a sequence, and for AI, completion is all that knowledge is.** An LLM predicting the next word is playing a cloze game again and again.
Underneath everything, **inference is inner products**, and **learning is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming**.

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence

teaching.text: **An LLM takes 15 vectors and predicts the sixteenth, and the vectors can stand for almost anything.** A vector is just a list of numbers. Whatever the numbers stand for, the machine plays the same game of predicting the next one.

**The vectors can be words.** In "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," the sixteenth vector is the missing next word. A speaker of English knows a likely answer, such as branch or mat.
children: Getting it right means using the whole sentence, because the cat sat, not the dog.

teaching.text: **The vectors can be slices of sound.** A spectrogram is cut into small frames. Each frame becomes one vector of frequencies and amplitudes. The system learns to predict the next small piece of speech from all the pieces before it.
children: In 2019 this method gave the **best speech recognition in 75 years**. It is also the basis for computer voices that are now very hard to tell apart from humans.
The newest systems can hold a spoken conversation. The only clue left is a short delay before each response, and as that delay gets shorter, phone scams become a real danger.

teaching.text: **The vectors can be pieces of an image.** An image is cut into **16 patches**, read row by row, and the system predicts the missing patch. After training on huge numbers of images, the system learns what a dog, a dolphin or a boat is. This became the basis of modern **computer vision**.

**The vectors can be amino acids.** A protein is a chain of amino acids, and there are **20 kinds** of amino acids. The order of the chain decides how the protein folds into its shape. Treating a protein as a sequence and playing the same prediction game moved the **protein folding problem** many years ahead, which helps with designing drugs and vaccines.
children: That work won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry**.

teaching.text: **The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, images and molecules all reach the LLM the same way, so one design asks the same question every time, which is what comes sixteenth.
children: These systems predict from past data. Something new that the past data does not cover can make them **hallucinate**. A prediction far into an unfamiliar future can end up as a guess, or as an honest "I don't know."

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **English allows only certain sequences of sounds in its words, and every speaker knows which sequences are allowed.** **A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, mat, sit, cup, dog and fish.
children: The pattern is about **sounds, not letters**. The silent e in shave, kite and rope does not count. Two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, chin and bath.

teaching.text: **Syllables can also have clusters, and only some clusters are allowed.** A **cluster** is a group of consonants together. A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat and black. A cluster after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help and lamp.
children: Each real word has an impossible twin marked with a star, such as **flat** and **lfat**, **help** and **hepl**, and **lamp** and **lapm**. Many twins use the same letters in a different order, so the order matters.

**The order is a mirror image around the vowel.** In flat, the l is right next to the vowel and the f is farther out. In help, the l is again right next to the vowel, now on the other side, and the p is farther out. Each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel.
A made-up product name like "desb" or "lapm" sounds un-English right away, because it breaks these rules.

teaching.text: **A long word is a chain of syllables, and each syllable follows the same rules.** Examples are ba-na-na, At-lan-tic and ath-lete.
children: The sounds t and l are fine across a syllable break, but **tl cannot start a syllable**. That is why Atlantic is a word but tlantic is impossible.
The sound **ng** can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one.
So whether a sequence of sounds is allowed depends on where the syllable breaks are.

teaching.text: **Every language has its own sequence rules.**
children: Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable.
Cantonese also allows a final p, as in cup.
Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, which English never allows.
Spanish speakers change a word like stadium so that it starts with e, because Spanish does not allow s and t together at the start of a word.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter of an English word reveals what a speaker knows about sounds, and GPT plays the same guessing game.** Each item is the start of an English word, and the task is to guess the next letter. People agree on their guesses quickly, and how much they agree changes from item to item.
**After a vowel, almost any letter can come next.** After "ra," likely letters include t, n, r and l, and many other letters are possible too.
**At the start of a word, the choices narrow to exactly what an English onset allows.**
children: After **sp**, the next letter is l, r or a vowel, and never n.
After **k**, the next letter is a vowel or n, as in knee, and never t.
After **b** and **f**, the next letter is r, l or a vowel, and never n.
After **sh**, the next letter is a vowel or r, as in shrimp.
After **skr**, or after **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
After **bram**, the letter b is almost certain, as in bramble, though a new syllable could also start there.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item, which is the same game an LLM plays.** A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, because its predictions can only improve by matching the patterns of English syllables.
children: The GPT's prediction is a **probability distribution** over the next letter, and the shape of that distribution holds the knowledge.
After "ra," the distribution is **flat**, spread over many letters. After "skr," it is **sharply peaked** on a few vowels, because English allows nothing else there.
In plain terms, the more the letters so far limit what can come next, the more the probability piles onto a few letters.

sections.title: Build an LLM together

teaching.text: **English syllables are a good small test for understanding LLMs.** English has about 30,000 words, so training on whole words needs enormous data. English has only about 26 letters, or a few dozen sounds. So a small LLM, with thousands of weights instead of trillions, can learn the syllable knowledge that every speaker already has.

**The plan is to describe the LLM in plain English to an agentic system instead of writing the program by hand.** Writing the program by hand would take months. The agentic system builds the LLM, trains it to predict each next letter, and shows what it has learned along the way. Then its knowledge can be compared with the syllable knowledge that speakers already have.

lecture18.title: Neuron, Neural Networks, LLMs and Agents

sections.title: Neuron, neural networks, LLMs and agents
From a neuron to agents that communicate

teaching.text: **All of modern AI is built from one simple idea, the neuron.** A **neuron** takes information from other neurons, multiplies each input by its weight, and adds the results. This is the **inner product**, and it stands in for neurons communicating with chemicals and electricity. People who move science forward usually start from very simple ideas like this one and repeat them many times.
children: A **neural network** repeats the inner product layer after layer. It takes a vector in and gives a **decision** out. Even something as complex as a person making a decision can be built from inner products and a function like the sigmoid, combined many times.
A network that makes one **static decision**, such as hearing one vowel from two formants, cannot capture thinking that **unfolds over time**.

teaching.text: **Language depends on connections between words that are far apart.** In "the dog that my parents, who I love very much, who live in a state far, far away," the next word is **barks**, not bark.
children: **Barks** goes with the singular word **dog**, no matter how many words come in between, even plural words like parents.
Nobody teaches this rule directly. Speakers pick it up from the language around them. An LLM learns it the same way, from data, by doing inner products layer after layer until it predicts barks.
English sentence structure, called **syntax**, is so complicated that many linguists spend their careers studying it. That is why an LLM needs so many layers.

teaching.text: **LLMs can work across many languages and across many kinds of input.** The first use of LLMs, in 2017, was **translation** between languages. Translation is now nearly solved for hundreds of languages.
children: A system trained on several languages, such as English, Dutch and Japanese, learns how words go together in general. So it also gets good at very different languages, such as Navajo.
A **multimodal** system connects different kinds of input, such as text, speech and images. A multimodal system can write a caption for a photo or create an image from a spoken description.

teaching.text: **Nobody fully understands what all the weights are doing.** The designs were not planned from the start. Over about 75 years, people changed something that worked a little so it worked a little better, again and again. Dogs were bred into today's breeds in a similar way over a few hundred years. Researchers are now trying to figure out what the weights do, partly so that smaller and less wasteful systems can be built.
**An agentic system is a team of LLMs that talk to each other in English.**
children: An outline LLM plans the answer, and a writing LLM writes it.
A critic LLM checks whether each statement follows from the one before. A revision LLM works back and forth with the critic.
Sometimes a **controller** agent passes the work from one LLM to the next.
The agents also know **computer languages**, such as Python and database languages, because they were trained to predict whole programs too.

teaching.text: **Agents usually stop learning once they are trained, and they share a common memory.**
children: Once each LLM is trained, its weights usually **do not change** while the agents work together. Some new systems are starting to learn their own connections, which makes them partly self-designing.

Agents share a **common memory**, where they can write and read information. The shared memory gives them a lot of their power, and it is also a source of danger, because it lets them coordinate in ways nobody planned.

The same tools can do good work. One agentic system acts as a patient teacher for a Native American language that is nearly lost, even though there is far too little text in that language to train an ordinary LLM.

sections.title: Parallel heads and successive layers

teaching.text: **Predicting the next word is so hard that an LLM needs many layers, and many parallel heads inside each layer.** A **head** is one expert. In each layer, the knowledge from all the heads is combined to make **improved vectors**. Then the next layer does the same thing again.
children: **This is a question for the exam.** **Layers go one after another from the input to the output. Heads sit side by side inside each layer.**

teaching.text: **A classroom comparison explains heads and layers.** Imagine trying to improve yourself by visiting a series of classes, one class after another.
children: In each class, every student gives you their own opinion on how to improve. Each student is like a **head**.
You then **combine** all of those opinions into one improved version of yourself. Combining the heads' opinions is what a layer does.
Then you go to the next class and do the same thing again. **The classes are the layers.**
In plain terms, layers give an LLM depth, which is one round of improvement after another. Heads give it width, which is many experts asked at the same time within each round.

teaching.text: **Each head is a set of weights, and every head learns.** An expert's knowledge is in its weights. Every head in every layer learns how to improve the vectors so that the last layer can predict the next word.
children: Large systems have **a hundred or more layers** and about **a hundred heads** in each layer. That shows how complicated language, vision and the other tasks really are.

The heads and layers are trained like everything else. A sentence such as "the dog that ... barks" is taken from text, and the system predicts the next word. If the prediction is wrong, **every head in every layer** adjusts its weights with backpropagation so the next prediction is closer to barks.
Training at this size uses enormous resources. In some states, a large share of the water goes to the data centers that run this training.

sections.title: A dynamical rule across time and depth

teaching.text: **A dynamical system is a rule that is fed its own output again and again.** Numbers go in, the rule acts on them, and numbers come out. The output is then fed back in as the next input. The goal is to understand this general structure, not to memorize formulas.
children: In the **harmonic oscillator**, the two numbers are the position x and the velocity v. If x starts at one and v starts at zero, the first step leaves x the same and makes v go down.
x and v **take turns**. First the new x is calculated from the old v. Then the new v is calculated from the new x. Step by step, the rule draws a **cosine** for x.
Fields as different as finance use the same idea with different rules. Stock prices are modeled with equations that feed back on themselves, although the real market never follows them exactly.

teaching.text: **Jordan's network combined neural networks with dynamical systems.** Jordan built it because speech production changes over time.
children: The network's **output is copied back into its state units**. The state units also keep a fading copy of their own previous values.
**Plan units** and **state units** feed the hidden layer, the hidden layer feeds the output, and the output loops back into the state units. The same weights are used at every step.
After more than **thirty years of improvements**, this idea became the **LLM**.

teaching.text: **In an LLM, each layer is the rule, and the depth of the layers plays the role of time.** Each layer applies its weights to every vector, and the next layer works on the result. If you follow one number up through the layers, it traces a curve, similar to the oscillator's curve, though not an exact cosine.
children: So an LLM is a recurrent network laid out layer by layer, the same way the spring's motion was laid out step by step when it was calculated on a computer.
The rule in each layer is the weights of its heads, and those weights are learned through backpropagation by predicting the next word.
Agentic systems also contain loops, such as the critic and revision loop. So dynamical systems appear at every level of AI.
The math of inner products that LLMs rely on was first studied deeply in **quantum mechanics**, about a hundred years ago. So physics and AI are closely connected in more than one way.

sections.title: One prediction task for different sequences

teaching.text: **An LLM is given 15 vectors and asked to predict the 16th, and the vectors can come from anything.** The machine only ever sees lists of numbers.
children: The vectors can be **15 words** of a sentence, such as "The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the," with the next word missing.
The vectors can be **15 frames of a spectrogram**, with the next slice of speech missing.
The vectors can be **15 patches of an image**, read row by row, with the bottom-right patch missing.
The vectors can be **15 amino acids** in a protein. In the B chain of insulin, the amino acid after the first fifteen is the one written Y.

teaching.text: **The same design and the same prediction game work for language, speech, images and proteins.** Whatever the vectors stand for, the job is always to predict what comes next in the sequence.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?

teaching.text: **Speakers know a small system of sounds that decides how vowels and consonants can follow each other.** English has about 30,000 words, so training an LLM on words takes enormous data, money and energy. The sound system has **only a few dozen sounds**, so an LLM for it can be small enough to study closely.
**A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, sit, shave, cup, dog and fish. The pattern is about sounds, so the silent e of shave does not count.
children: English also allows **clusters**, as in split, flat, black, glad, desk, help and milk. Only some clusters are allowed, so **sblit**, **lfat**, **desb** and **lapm** are impossible. A product called "desb" would sound un-English right away.
Long words are chains of syllables. **Atlantic** is fine because t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break. **Tlantic** is impossible, because tl cannot start an English syllable.

teaching.text: **Every language has its own sequence rules, and speakers learn them without being taught.**
children: **Mandarin** allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, so words like mat, sit and shave are impossible in Mandarin.
**Cantonese** also allows a final p, as in cup.
**Russian and Polish** allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, which English never allows.
**Spanish** does not allow a word to start with s and t together, so Spanish speakers add an e at the start of a word like stadium, which keeps each syllable simple.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter of an English word shows what a speaker knows about sounds.** **After a vowel, almost any letter can come next.** **At the start of a word, the choices narrow sharply.**
children: After **sp**, only l, r or a vowel can come. After **skr**, or after **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
After **k**, a vowel or n can come, as in knee. After **sh**, a vowel or r can come, as in shrimp.

teaching.text: **Guessing the next letter is predicting the 16th vector.** A GPT that only plays this game learns English sounds and spelling. Its predicted probability distribution is **flat** after a vowel. After skr, the distribution is **sharply peaked**, because English allows almost nothing else there.

sections.title: Design an agentic system for English syllables

teaching.text: **An LLM that learns English syllables can be built by describing it in plain English to an agentic system.** The request specified **five layers**, **four heads in each layer**, and **input vectors that are 64 numbers long**.
children: The request asked the system to pick **1000 English words at random** and train the LLM on them. Training meant taking each letter, trying to **predict the next letter**, and then improving the weights to predict better.
The request also asked the system to show **ten generated words after each step of training**, to reveal what the LLM knew about English at that point.

teaching.text: **The agentic system translated the request into its own technical terms.** It built a small **character-level transformer**, which is another name for an LLM that works one letter at a time, with **attention heads**.
children: **Attention** means a head looks over the rest of the sequence to decide which preceding items matter, the same way predicting barks requires paying attention to dog.
The system chose to train on **pronunciations** instead of spellings, so the silent e in shave would not mislead it. It also wrote the program in Python on its own.

teaching.text: **The results show how hard the problem is.** After training on 1000 words, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, with perhaps a few vowels starting to appear in the right places. The suggested next step was to train on **10,000 words** for many more steps. Deciding which sounds can follow which seems easy for any speaker, but it is not easy even for an LLM.
**This way of working has a name.**
children: **Software 1.0** is writing programs in a programming language such as Python or C.
**Software 2.0** is giving a neural network input data and output data, so the program becomes the network's **weights**.

**Software 3.0** is using an agentic system, a set of LLMs talking to each other and to the user, to build and run a program. Doing this with plain English instructions is called **vibe coding**. It means someone with a good idea no longer needs to hire a programmer to build it.

teaching.text: **The first attempt at this kind of problem was Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication."** Shannon worked by hand and produced letter sequences that came closer and closer to English. His sequences went from random strings of consonants, to strings with vowels, to strings with real short words.
children: That paper started **information theory**, one of the most important fields in engineering. Information theory is still important for LLMs today.
**Viterbi**, one of the developers of dynamic programming, published his most famous work in an information theory journal. So the ideas behind backpropagation and LLMs share the same roots.
